#9589. How Bosnia's ACX Crypto Exchange Went From Big Promises to a Regulatory Ban

Investigating the nexus of digital power, state surveillance, public money, and Kremlin influence in the Western Balkans and beyond.

Investigating the nexus of digital power, state surveillance, public money, and Kremlin influence in the Western Balkans and beyond.

Investigating the nexus of digital power, state surveillance, public money, and Kremlin influence in the Western Balkans and beyond.

He promised a new crypto era. Customers lost access to their own money.

On August 14, 2026, Republika Srpska’s Securities Commission ordered ACX operator Adria Technology removed from its virtual-currency service-provider register for one year. The commission’s August 14, 2026, decision documenting failures to cooperate with inspectors and financial-compliance violations exposed the gulf between the exchange’s grand promises of security and the reality of its conduct.

The regulatory expulsion came after months of inaccessible accounts, desperate customer complaints, blocked company bank accounts, criminal reports, and a creditor’s successful lawsuit. Yet in Banja Luka, even obtaining a court judgment against the exchange did not mean obtaining payment.

Republika Srpska is one of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s two constituent entities, adjoining Croatia and therefore the European Union. The ACX collapse exposes a brazen accountability gap on Europe’s doorstep: a crypto operator can lock customers out of their funds, ignore regulators, evade court process servers, and still walk completely free.

At the center of the scandal stands Branko Petrović: a decorated Police Academy graduate in Banja Luka, a former Interior Ministry officer, a crypto exchange founder peddling fantasies of multimillion-mark foreign investments, an exposed fraudster under prosecutorial investigation, and, most absurdly of all, a recurring media authority on cybersecurity.

His police credentials helped him build trust. The paralyzed institutions of Republika Srpska allowed him to betray it with impunity.

The police connection is documented, and Petrović turned it into the cornerstone of his public authority.

In its September 22, 2017, report on the graduation of Banja Luka’s eighteenth Police Academy class, RTRS identified Petrović among the leading cadets. Branko Petrović from Ugljevik and Sanja Tomić from Bijeljina were singled out as the best among 131 graduates entering the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska, known as MUP RS.

Petrović told the public broadcaster that being among the top cadets was a great honor. The institution’s stated mission was to produce officers capable of protecting citizens and their property from crime.

His later business biography weaponized that law-enforcement pedigree for commercial credibility. A Jahorina Economic Forum biography reviewed on October 27, 2026, describing Petrović’s police service and ACX career notes that he served in the police force for several years before moving into cloud engineering, digital forensics, and cybersecurity, ultimately founding ACX.

In promotional appearances, Petrović routinely advertised himself as a cybersecurity specialist who worked on international projects and trained law-enforcement agencies and public institutions in investigating high-tech crime and cryptocurrency fraud.

The irony is staggering. A former police officer who built his reputation claiming to teach institutions how to track cybercriminals became the director of a crypto exchange whose own customers could not retrieve their money.

Behind the slick ACX and ACX+ branding sits a financially gutted legal entity: Adria Technology d.o.o. Banja Luka.

The CompanyWall profile reviewed on October 27, 2026, identifying Adria Technology’s registration, management, and owners lists its establishment date as September 2, 2023, its tax identifier as 4405119460004, and its registration number as 57–01–0435–23. Petrović serves as the company’s director alongside co-owners Nikola Maričić and Ankkom d.o.o.

While Petrović was touring regional conferences posing as a fintech visionary, the company’s financial reality was a disaster. Public financial filings put Adria Technology’s 2025 revenue at just BAM 176,193. BAM is the convertible mark, Bosnia and Herzegovina’s currency.

Against that modest revenue, the company recorded a 2025 loss of approximately BAM 219,500 and negative equity of approximately BAM 89,800, with just five employees and blocked bank accounts.

The brand promised a financial empire. The balance sheet showed a collapsing shell.

Petrović’s media buildup began long before users realized their funds were trapped.

A CAPITAL article published March 18, 2022, promoting Petrović’s Educor platform and MF banka support presented him as a rising young entrepreneur who had secured a BAM 10,000 grant. ACX was then publicly unveiled at a Banja Luka crypto conference on September 22, 2023, and Adria Technology entered the regulator’s virtual-currency register that November.

Then came the headline number designed to dazzle local investors and ordinary citizens alike.

In its June 3, 2024, report announcing a BAM 6.3 million Modulus investment in ACX, CAPITAL promoted a story that an American technology giant was pouring millions into the Banja Luka exchange. The article quoted Modulus CEO Richard Gardner praising ACX’s team and featured Petrović promising capabilities unseen on other domestic platforms.

Petrović promised hundreds of cryptocurrency trading pairs, regional dominance, a cutting-edge trading platform, institutional Fireblocks wallet security, and access to global investors. He explicitly boasted of strict electronic customer verification, transaction monitoring, certified anti-money-laundering personnel, and top-tier information-security standards.

Every single one of those compliance boasts would later be demolished by regulators.

By April 2025, the hype escalated further. Finticipate’s April 30, 2025, speaker promotion presented Petrović as ACX Bank’s founder and an innovator behind ACX Token, even though the company held no banking license and offered zero bank-deposit protection.

By October 2025, Petrović was aggressively pitching company tokenization, token design, white papers, and sales through “ACX+.” He was selling the public an expanding financial future right as the trap was closing on his existing customers’ money.

A press release about BAM 6.3 million was easy to publish. Returning customers’ actual deposits proved another matter entirely.

Petrović later tried to blame the freeze on a technical migration, but the documented timeline destroys that excuse. Customers were being denied their money while the platform was still online.

In Svjetlana Šurlan’s May 15, 2026, Bloomberg Adria investigation into ACX customer lawsuits and criminal-police complaints, Banja Luka company Rocket Science revealed that it had repeatedly demanded payouts starting in December 2025.

Only after threatening legal action did the company extract partial payments in February and March 2026. The remainder of its money never arrived.

Rocket Science’s attorney, Davorin Marinković, confirmed that the company sued Adria Technology on February 11, 2026, pursuing approximately BAM 35,000 by May and petitioning the court to freeze the exchange’s bank funds. Petrović himself was forced to admit that the corporate client had demanded its money while the platform was still operating.

On January 15, 2026, the curtain fell for everyone else. Customers were suddenly locked out of the platform, fed classic stalling stories about “technical upgrades” and “system migration.”

Retail users told Bloomberg that savings of BAM 1,200 to BAM 1,500 were completely inaccessible. Others described a wall of silence, ignored withdrawal requests, and the ultimate absurdity: an exchange asking its own customers to tell support how much money they believed they had in their accounts.

ACX was not merely refusing to pay out funds. It was acting as if it no longer even had a ledger of what it owed.

With institutions silent and media outlets looking the other way, victims had to build their own public warning system.

The Crypto.ba thread opened April 29, 2026, documenting customers’ frozen assets and failed attempts to contact ACX reads like a textbook anatomy of a crypto exit scam.

A user named “Djuro” detailed months of locked funds, a dead website, a disconnected phone line, and futile attempts to reach Petrović across multiple channels. On May 5, user “bigmoney77” reported the exact same pattern: occasional stalling emails promising a glorious return, paired with broken promises to pay out fiat currency or transfer crypto to external wallets.

When Djuro physically went to ACX’s Banja Luka offices to demand answers, he was initially fed empty assurances, only to return later and discover that the company had quietly vacated the premises. By May 7, he was filing complaints with the Securities Commission.

The forum record shows that only those who threatened immediate legal action or relentlessly hounded Petrović for months stood a chance of seeing a cent. On May 19, user “BL3CK” reported extracting payment only after serving a formal pre-litigation notice. In Crypto.ba posts dated July 13 and August 6, 2026, describing a negotiated recovery after months of pursuit, Djuro recounted that it took six grueling months of messages, calls, and physical visits to finally force a payout.

Less aggressive users were simply left behind. On July 28, Haris Mustafić reported that his inquiries regarding roughly 350 platform tokens worth around BAM 700 were completely ignored.

In Branko Petrović’s “new era of crypto,” customer withdrawals had been replaced by an endurance test of harassment and legal threats.

When Bloomberg Adria finally confronted Petrović in May 2026, his web of deceptions unraveled in real time.

Petrović first lied to reporters, claiming he knew of no lawsuits against the company or its founders. Only after journalists confronted him with the exact details of the Rocket Science lawsuit did he admit the case existed and that a court hearing had already taken place.

To explain why user funds had been held hostage since January, Petrović spun a convoluted global tale. He claimed ACX had lost access to Modulus Global’s source code after the American partner sold its crypto division to an unnamed Australian firm. He blamed an Italian auditor for objecting to investments in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and claimed BitGo had rejected ACX in February 2026, forcing his team to build its own custody system in mid-March to avoid paying alternative providers EUR 60,000 a year.

Crucially, Petrović had never told his trapped customers a single word about losing his technology partner or lacking a custody system during the four months their money was frozen. They were only told after journalists exposed the crisis on May 15.

Even his attempt to prove that ACX was communicating with users blew up in his face. When Petrović sent Bloomberg screenshots of customer support emails as “proof” of responsiveness, reporters noticed that half of the emails had been sent on the exact day Bloomberg’s questions landed in his inbox.

He was manufacturing an alibi while his users stared at a dead website.

Nothing strips away the fraud of ACX’s “multimillion-mark” image quite like the records of Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Indirect Taxation Authority.

On April 23, 2026, tax authorities ordered the suspension of all transactions through Adria Technology’s bank accounts over an unpaid tax debt of just BAM 3,783. The blockade took effect on April 24.

On May 14, Petrović brushed off the blockade to reporters, claiming the tax debt would be paid “in the coming days.” He also insisted that blocked bank accounts did not stop him from returning users’ assets because customer funds were held in cryptocurrency, not fiat currency.

That excuse exposed the core lie of the entire operation: if the cryptocurrency was sitting safely in wallets outside the blocked bank accounts, why wasn’t Petrović returning it to the owners?

Even worse was what happened to the tax bill. By July 7, Central Bank records showed Adria Technology’s accounts were still blocked. By August 21, the tax authority confirmed the debt, including interest, stood at BAM 3,775.

In four months, the total net reduction of the original tax balance was BAM 8.

The man who went on television and business portals bragging about a BAM 6.3 million American investment could not or would not pay a BAM 3,783 tax debt, reducing it by just eight marks across an entire summer.

With regulators breathing down his neck and bank accounts frozen, Petrović kept buying time by promising a grand comeback under the ACX+ banner.

Bloomberg Adria’s May 27, 2026, report on ACX’s proposed relaunch during regulatory supervision and blocked accounts documented how the company quietly scrubbed its newer domain and reverted to its old web address, promising a full relaunch on June 23.

Ivana Raonić’s May 28, 2026, Bloomberg Adria newsletter on ACX’s announced return captured the sheer audacity of Petrović’s marketing: even with accounts blocked and police complaints filed, ACX was proclaiming that “a new era of crypto trading” was arriving in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

On July 6, ACX announced a “beta version.” It was a Potemkin village. Some users logged in only to find wiped-out, empty balances; others could not log in at all. More importantly, ACX informed users that bank deposits and withdrawals would remain disabled throughout July, pushing the promise of normal operations to August.

Putting up a login screen where victims could look at frozen numbers was not a relaunch. It was a stalling tactic.

While Petrović was playing software developer with his “beta” platform, the courts were ruling against him, and he was actively evading the law.

Bloomberg Adria’s July 4, 2026, newsletter on the implications of ACX’s first reported judgment and Šurlan’s July 8, 2026, investigation into Rocket Science’s successful case and ACX’s restricted beta relaunch laid bare the company’s courtroom defeat.

On June 15, 2026, Banja Luka’s District Commercial Court issued a default judgment against Adria Technology after Petrović’s company didn’t even bother to respond to Rocket Science’s lawsuit. The court ordered Adria Technology to pay USD 26,000 in convertible mark equivalent, plus interest dating back to November 2025 and legal costs, within 30 days.

What happened next shows utter contempt for the legal system.

By August, repeated official attempts to serve the court judgment on Adria Technology had failed, including an attempt carried out with the assistance of MUP RS police officers. On August 21, the defrauded creditor was forced to beg the court to post the judgment on the courthouse notice board because Petrović’s company could not be reached.

How does a former top MUP RS cadet, who gives public interviews to Banja Luka journalists and walks freely around the city, suddenly become a ghost whom the court and his former police colleagues cannot locate to serve a USD 26,000 judgment?

He tried the exact same disappearing act with financial regulators, and it finally cost ACX its legal existence.

On August 14, 2026, the Securities Commission of Republika Srpska issued its decision kicking Adria Technology out of the virtual-currency register. The commission’s August 14, 2026, meeting record specifying the duration of the exclusion confirmed the one-year ban, which followed the commission’s May 27, 2026, public notice explaining virtual-currency registration and anti-money-laundering supervision.

The regulator’s findings read like an indictment of a rogue operation. When inspectors tried to conduct supervision, Adria Technology obstructed them at every turn: failing to grant unobstructed access to company premises, withholding required documentation, failing to ensure the presence of authorized personnel, and refusing to grant inspectors access to the trading application itself.

Furthermore, the company had failed to conduct mandatory risk assessments for 2024 and 2025 and violated anti-money-laundering laws by failing to properly verify customer identities, business relationships, residences, and the origin of funds. Every compliance standard Petrović had bragged about in the media was a lie.

When the commission mailed its supervision report on July 13, Adria Technology simply refused to pick up the mail. The regulator had to send electronic copies on July 23, July 24, and July 28.

Bloomberg Adria’s August 28, 2026, report on ACX’s exclusion and statutory violations confirmed that stripping Adria Technology from the register made it completely illegal for ACX to operate.

Even after being banned by the regulator on August 14, Petrović tried to deceive the public one last time about why ACX was shutting down.

On August 26, twelve days after the Securities Commission had already ordered his company removed from the register, Petrović posted a shutdown notice claiming that ACX had voluntarily submitted a request for deregistration that very day and was shutting down of its own accord.

It was a blatant fabrication of the timeline: you cannot quit a register two weeks after you have already been thrown out of it for breaking the law.

In the ACX shutdown statement carrying an August 25, 2026, dateline and reviewed on October 27, 2026, Petrović had the audacity to play the victim. He blamed “inadequate regulation,” high development costs, and “certain interest groups connected to media in BiH,” whining that media reporting had triggered a wave of customers demanding their money back.

To a conman, journalists exposing frozen accounts and victims asking for their own savings back are a hostile conspiracy.

The statement claimed that 821 out of 902 users had been paid off and promised that everyone else would be settled by a “planned” deadline of October 1.

Predictably, that deadline was just another lie. In Crypto.ba posts dated September 23 and October 1, 2026, recording missed callbacks and the planned repayment deadline, defrauded users documented that promised 48-hour callbacks never happened and their money had still not been returned as October arrived.

While Bloomberg Adria (alongside brief pickups by BL Portal on May 15, 2026, regarding user lawsuits and on July 8, 2026, regarding Adria Technology’s court defeat) was documenting Petrović’s collapse, the rest of the media scene in Republika Srpska maintained a deafening silence.

Worse than silence, however, was active image laundering by one of the region’s best-known independent business portals: CAPITAL.ba.

Giving Petrović a microphone in a November 6, 2025, CAPITAL TV podcast report presenting him as a cybersecurity and digital-forensics expert was bad enough in hindsight. What CAPITAL did on July 31, 2026, is an unforgivable journalistic disgrace.

In Andrijana Pisarević’s July 31, 2026, CAPITAL report on hackers taking more than BAM 500,000 from Republika Srpska retail chains, the outlet once again featured Branko Petrović as a respected “cybersecurity and digital-forensics expert.”

Look at the calendar. By July 31, 2026, Petrović’s ACX exchange had been holding customer funds hostage for over six months. His company’s bank accounts had been blocked by tax authorities for three months. Criminal complaints had already been sent to prosecutors. And just three weeks earlier, the Banja Luka court judgment ordering his company to pay USD 26,000 to a defrauded client had been publicly reported.

Yet CAPITAL called Branko Petrović to lecture the public on how criminals abuse trust, manipulate payment instructions, and steal money from businesses.

Not a single word in CAPITAL’s article mentioned that their featured “expert” was the director of ACX, a man actively hiding from court servers and locking citizens out of their money. Instead of investigating a massive financial scandal in its own backyard, an independent outlet handed the perpetrator a megaphone to polish his credibility.

The paper trail of lawlessness is now sitting on the desks of police and prosecutors.

In Bloomberg Adria’s August 27, 2026, investigation into prosecutorial cases, failed judgment service, and ACX’s closure, MUP RS confirmed that criminal-police officers submitted a formal report regarding ACX to the District Public Prosecutor’s Office in Banja Luka on May 28, followed by a supplemental report on July 2.

The Securities Commission also forwarded victim complaints to both MUP RS and the Financial Intelligence Department of the State Investigation and Protection Agency, SIPA. The Banja Luka Prosecutor’s Office confirmed that it received three separate reports regarding Adria Technology, formed criminal files, and opened investigations.

When confronted with the prosecutorial investigation in August, Petrović arrogantly remarked that opening a file does not mean a crime was committed, and boasted that police assisting with court judgment delivery is not a criminal sanction. He brazenly refused to answer why neither the court nor the police could find him to hand him that judgment.

And that brings us to the question that every defrauded citizen and every honest observer in Bosnia and Herzegovina is asking today: Why is Branko Petrović still a free man?

How does an individual take money and cryptocurrency from hundreds of citizens, lock the doors of his exchange in January, ignore tax blocks for months, lock out state financial inspectors, refuse to collect official mail, evade court enforcement with police assistance, get banned by the regulator for breaking the law, miss his own October 1 repayment deadline, and still stroll untouched through Banja Luka in late October 2026?

Where did the customers’ cryptocurrency and money actually go during the nine months their accounts were frozen? Which wallets did Petrović control, and whose pockets did those assets line while Adria Technology claimed to be broke over a BAM 3,783 tax bill?

Most importantly, who inside the police and judicial apparatus of Republika Srpska is shielding a former star cadet of the Banja Luka Police Academy from handcuffs?

When an ordinary citizen owes a fraction of that money, enforcement is swift and ruthless. When an insider with a police pedigree and media friends runs a crypto trap in Banja Luka, prosecutors spend months “conducting investigations” while the perpetrator goes on portals to give advice on cybercrime.

A shutdown notice on a dead website does not erase a robbery. Customers were never asking Branko Petrović for a new financial era. They are asking for their stolen money back, and for the prosecutors to finally do their job.

#9588. Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

#9587. nemotron-halloween

TL;DR: MonsterHouse is an interactive projection I created for Halloween. He listens to trick-or-treaters, answers in the voice of a grumpy old pirate ship and softens when visitors remember their manners. He is built on the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent with NVIDIA Nemotron ASR, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, Magpie TTS Zeroshot and Audio2Face-3D, and he runs on a single workstation.

I wanted the kids visiting my house at Halloween to interact in a fun and unique way. The house was going to be in charge and giving out the treats, but more grumpy than scary. Somehow, my solution was to give the garage door a mouth and teach him to complain.

That became MonsterHouse: a grumpy old building with pirate stories, a fiery grin and a suspicious weakness for “please.” NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent supplies the conversation foundation. Nemotron Speech does the listening, Bolt E4B is the brain, NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot is the live voice, and NVIDIA Audio2Face-3D makes the wooden mouth talk.

The mouth came first. I imagined the wooden garage door boards splitting into jagged lips, with the burning flames of hell illuminating the driveway from beyond whenever he opened his cursed mouth. He needed to look ancient, expressive and mildly offended by the existence of visitors.

A few expressions from a house with plenty to say.

Creating a custom animation rig was one of the more labor intensive parts of the build. After bashing it into submission, I could export the facial expression shapes that Audio2Face-3D could later animate. The character SkelMesh was built in Autodesk Maya then exported into Unreal Engine where virtual fire and effects were added behind the door. With no eyes, no eyebrows and no blinking, he’s a surprisingly economical monster.

While all the nonsense of building the character was going on, NVIDIA built the Nemotron Voice Agent. What was supposed to be the hard part of the build now became rather fun, iterative and easy. I had a foundation for listening, conversation and speech right out of the box. The house already had a mouth. Now he could finally find something to complain about.

The house needed a past as cantankerous as its personality so I devised a backstory that the house had been built from the timbers of a sunken pirate ship, haunted by its stormy past. The nautical complaints now had a reason. This was the ship, reincarnated as real estate and not entirely pleased about it.

The performance needed a guide, a path to follow from greeting to goodbye while providing treats along the way. First, the house would brush visitors off with remarks like “I’m busy grumbling, go bother the neighbors!” But persistence would wear him down. A “Please” could break through immediately, and “thank you” earned a warm farewell. Once a visitor won him over, I wanted him to stay won over. Nobody wants to negotiate with the same garage door twice.

Here is where the Voice Agent really shines. You can choose any LLM you like. Because I wanted the system to be off-grid and completely self-contained, I had a memory and compute budget.

The character needs more than a prompt that says “be grumpy.” It had to follow a master conversation flow, respond to what visitors actually said, track encounter state, and leave enough compute for the rest of the pipeline.

After testing more than a dozen models, I landed on Bolt E4B to supply the live dialogue. It is an open small language model purpose-built for local conversational agents and interactive characters, which is a fair description of a talking garage door. I use the 4-bit quantized release (the “4GB” in its name) as the default response model, with the BF16 checkpoint available for comparison.

If it’s not obvious by now, I work at NVIDIA and due to this I was able to test Bolt E4B before its public release and found it to be a solid choice, with a smaller footprint than other frontrunners- Qwen3 30B-A3B and Qwen 3.6 35B-A3B.

It works inside the Nemotron Voice Agent pipeline, turning what visitors say into the next suitably reluctant reply.

Bolt provides the conversational foundation. My prompts, application logic and LoRA adapter trained on thousands of reviewed example conversations shape it into this particular stubborn ship.

Creating a dataset of over 5000 multi-turn conversations meant I could train LoRAs for each model I felt good enough to be an option. Some took about an hour to train, some took a couple. A local agent ran everything and benchmarked the results. That agent and a very large LLM created and judged the dataset to begin with. This happened at night or while I was doing the day job.

With the LoRA in place I check the replies for continuity, timing and tone, benchmark models and adapters for quality, repetition and speed, and then listen to the performance. The house should give in eventually, without turning into a cheerful concierge. A little resistance is part of the charm. An endless argument with a garage door is not.

Two shortcuts, two outputs. Authored text skips fresh dialogue generation, and saved audio skips synthesis. Clean speech drives the animation separately from the audience effects.

A haunted house loses authority if he takes too long to complain. The pipeline releases speakable text before an entire answer is finished, so the house can start talking while the rest of the sentence is still on its way. Prepared greetings and candy jokes cover familiar encounters: the text bank saves language-model work, and cached recordings save speech synthesis. Even an ancient grump benefits from rehearsing.

NVIDIA Magpie TTS Zeroshot turns text into the Queen’s English. Its zero-shot voice conditioning uses a short reference sample instead of a trained voice; mine supplies the grumpy pirate character. The house has seven moods, from grumpy and menacing to amused and delighted, and emotion tags dictated by the prompt template and provided by the LLM choose how each line is delivered. Since each emotion requires a different 3-10 second voice sample I added a “Sample your Voice” block on the UI’s tool tab. I could then read and record a sample line of text in my best happy pirate or angry pirate voice. When it’s “Go” time, Bolt E4B decides what to say, and Magpie turns that text into speech with the proper delight or despair.

Next down the pipe is Audio2Face-3D and the 3d character scene I created in Epic’s Unreal Engine. The default model weights work best with a clean neutral male or female voice, not too deep, not too high (choose the appropriate gendered model for your use case). I wanted the house to have a very deep and demonic voice with echo and chamber. In this case, since my voice samples don’t have that theatrical heft, it’s actually a benefit. Audio2Face-3D gets clean speech from the samples and a second audio stream adds adjustable real-time vocal effects that play out the speakers.

To keep everything running smoothly, I split the work to a pair of GPUs: the language and voice model pipeline runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q, and Unreal Engine graphics with Audio2Face-3D runs on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell. Memory isn’t the issue, compute is. I want to keep animation at a consistent frame rate regardless of what processing the agent pipeline is doing.

Voice, animation and effects have to land together. A convincing monster needs more than a fast answer; it needs to sound as though the complaint belongs to the building. In my case, he does. Tweaks to sync audio delivery are available. I’ve found I could set them and forget them. (100ms compensates for the Audio2Face-3D buffering)

Somewhere along the way, “make the house talk” required an interface full of controls. I can audition cached lines, adjust the opening mood, follow the conversation, change the voice treatment and tune the mouth animation. Tabs cover conversations, model selection, recordings, prompts, performance monitoring and camera feeds, and a soundboard and custom dialogue field let me put words in his mouth. There are also model-loading controls and an Unreal Engine connection indicator, because sometimes the monster is not sulking. He is disconnected.

The MonsterHouse control desk, with the soundboard, custom lines, opening mood and conversation flow.

The fire and glow have joined the act. Editable rules tie visual cues to delivery: live cues begin with speech, while recorded performances can follow a saved timeline. I can direct a change of mood without rebuilding the scene.

Live mode runs the trick-or-treat character. Demo mode persuades The house to explain himself. Microphone mode lets me speak through the house directly, bypassing recognition, dialogue generation and speech synthesis. My clean voice drives the mouth; the audience hears the treated version. The house considers this possession. I consider it a useful fallback.

NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano Omni is a VLM that gives the house visual context. As an optional observer, it interprets camera images and describes visible costumes so the character has something specific to react to. Not looking to reinvent every wheel, I chose the popular object detection and tracking models YOLO and ByteTrack to count and track people currently in view. Keeping those jobs separate lets the house notice a group without asking Omni to narrate every frame.

For a suitably ridiculous test, I gave Omni a video of five costumed sheep at the door. Its saved analysis identified the pirate, vampire, witch, pumpkin and ghost outfits. That is the sort of visual context I want the house to use. Apparently even livestock have more elaborate Halloween plans than I do.

Five very woolly trick-or-treaters in a synthetic test replay. Costume labels come from the saved Omni analysis; boxes and track IDs are illustrative.

The sheep are a synthetic test, not evidence of a successful Halloween night. Real driveway groups, costumes and night lighting still need testing. Detection does trigger automatic greetings, but I fear trendy costume identification and suitably witty retorts may need some post training. Since the house has no eyes, he calls his visitor awareness echolocation. I am letting him have that one.

There is more to do: the animation can always improve, complete performance testing needs real visitors, and candy will one day be provided automatically. I have not yet reached the original goal of leaving him to run Halloween while I head off with my family to see the other neighborhood ghouls. But that is still the point of all this. One day a child will meet a grumpy old house, try a little kindness and discover that the old timber has a soft spot. And gives out candy bars.

The MonsterHouse code itself is not packaged for release, but every NVIDIA model it uses is available today, and the NVIDIA Nemotron Voice Agent gets you most of the way. This is the path I would follow.

A cached response bank and saved audio for your most common lines will make even a slow monster feel quick. In fact, if you happen to be limited by computing power, there is no reason why you can’t have a Live version that just uses Nemotron 3 ASR, a python conversation router, with all cached audio. You can use the Bolt E4B and Magpie pipeline to generate 100s of responses offline, then use the cache for the show. I’ll be doing this for the interactive pumpkins.

#9585. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing



There are lots of questions floating around about how affiliate marketing works, what to do and what not to do when it comes to setting up a business. With so much uncertainty surrounding both personal and business aspects of affiliate marketing. In this post, we will answer the most frequently asked question about affiliate marketing

1. What is affiliate marketing?

 Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!


2. What is an affiliate program?

 An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

3. What is an affiliate network and how do affiliate networks make money? 

 Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

4. What's the difference between affiliate marketing and dropshipping?

 Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

 5. Can affiliate marketing and performance marketing be considered the same thing?

 Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

 6. Is it possible to promote affiliate offers on mobile devices?

 Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

7. Where do I find qualified publishers?

 The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

8. What is an affiliate disclosure statement?

 An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

 9. Does social media activity play a significant role in affiliate marketing?

 Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

10. What is a super affiliate?

 A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

11. How do we track publisher sales activity?

 Publishers can be identified by their publisher ID, which is used in tracking cookies to determine which publishers generate sales. The activity is then viewed within a network's dashboard.

 12. Could we set up an affiliate program in multiple countries?

 Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

13. How can affiliate marketing help my business?

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

  •  It allows you to save time and money on marketing, which frees you up to focus on other aspects of your business.
  •  You get access to friendly marketers who are eager to help you succeed. 
  • It also helps you to promote your products by sharing links and banners with a new audience.
  •  It offers high ROI(Return on investment) and is cost-effective.

 14. How do I find quality publishers?

 One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

15. How Can we Promote Affiliate Links?

 Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

  • A website or blog
  • Through email marketing and newsletter
  • Social media, like Facebook, Instagram, or Twitter.
  •  Leave a comment on blogs or forums.
  • Write an e-book or other digital product.
  • Youtube

 16. Do you have to pay to sign up for an affiliate program?

 To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

17. What is a commission rate?

 Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Who manages your affiliate program?

 Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

18. What is a cookie?

 Cookies are small pieces of data that work with web browsers to store information such as user preferences, login or registration data, and shopping cart contents. When someone clicks on your affiliate link, a cookie is placed on the user's computer or mobile device. That cookie is used to remember the link or ad that the visitor clicked on. Even if the user leaves your site and comes back a week later to make a purchase, you will still get credit for the sale and receive a commission it depends on the site cookies duration

19. How long do cookies last?

 The merchant determines the duration of a cookie, also known as its “cookie life.” The most common length for an affiliate program is 30 days. If someone clicks on your affiliate link, you’ll be paid a commission if they purchase within 30 days of the click.

Final Saying

Most new affiliates are eager to begin their affiliate marketing business. Unfortunately, there is a lot of bad information out there that can lead inexperienced affiliates astray. Hopefully, the answer to your question will provide clarity on how affiliate marketing works and the pitfalls you can avoid. Most importantly, keep in mind that success in affiliate marketing takes some time. Don't be discouraged if you're not immediately making sales or earning money. It takes most new affiliates months to make a full-time income.

#9583. Why Crypto-Backed Lending Is Becoming Financial Infrastructure

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

For much of crypto’s history, digital assets have been treated primarily as something to buy, sell, trade, or transfer.

As the market matures, Bitcoin and other digital assets are increasingly being integrated into financial products that look less like speculative crypto applications and more like familiar financial infrastructure. One of the clearest examples is crypto-backed lending.

The basic concept is not particularly exotic. A borrower pledges an asset as collateral and receives liquidity against a portion of its value. Traditional finance has operated this way for decades through mortgages, securities-backed lending, equipment financing, and other forms of collateralized credit.

What changes with crypto is the infrastructure required to make the model work.

Digital assets trade continuously, can move sharply in price, can be transferred nearly instantly, and require an entirely different approach to custody. Building a functional lending market around them therefore requires a combination of traditional credit principles and technology capable of managing collateral in real time.

That combination is turning crypto-backed lending into something more interesting than another niche crypto product.

A person can own a valuable asset without having much liquid capital available.

A homeowner may have substantial equity tied up in a property. A business owner may have wealth concentrated in a company. An investor may hold a portfolio of securities they do not want to sell simply because they need cash.

Traditional finance developed lending products specifically to solve this problem.

Crypto holders increasingly face the same situation.

Someone who has accumulated Bitcoin over several years may need liquidity for a business investment, real estate purchase, tax obligation, diversification opportunity, or other expense. Selling cryptocurrency provides the cash, but it also reduces exposure to the asset.

Collateralized lending creates another option.

Instead of selling the asset, the borrower can pledge it as collateral and borrow against a portion of its value.

The economic concept is familiar. The technology required to manage it is not.

Traditional consumer lending often emphasizes credit history, income, employment, and the borrower's expected ability to make payments.

Collateralized crypto lending shifts much more attention toward the asset securing the loan.

The central measurement is loan-to-value, or LTV.

If a borrower pledges $200,000 worth of cryptocurrency and receives a $100,000 loan, the starting LTV is 50%.

From that point forward, the value of the collateral matters continuously.

If the cryptocurrency appreciates, the loan becomes increasingly overcollateralized. If the value falls, LTV rises. At predetermined thresholds, the borrower may need to provide additional collateral, repay part of the loan, or otherwise bring the position back within acceptable parameters.

This is where software becomes essential.

Crypto markets do not close at 4 p.m. They operate continuously across exchanges and jurisdictions. A collateral-management system therefore needs reliable pricing data, automated monitoring, predefined risk thresholds, and rapid communication with borrowers.

The lending product is inseparable from the technology monitoring it.

One of the most common objections to crypto-backed lending is that cryptocurrency is too volatile to function as reliable collateral.

But volatility does not necessarily prevent an asset from being financed.

It changes how conservatively that asset has to be financed.

More volatile collateral generally requires lower initial LTVs, greater collateral buffers, closer monitoring, and clearer procedures for dealing with rapid price declines.

This is fundamentally a risk-engineering problem.

A lender does not need Bitcoin to behave like cash or a Treasury bond. It needs systems capable of measuring the risk Bitcoin actually presents and structuring credit accordingly.

The same principle appears throughout finance.

Different assets receive different advance rates because their liquidity, volatility, market depth, and expected recovery values differ.

Crypto simply pushes the requirement for real-time risk management much further than most traditional collateral classes.

There is another complication that makes digital-asset lending structurally different from conventional credit: custody.

With traditional collateral, ownership and control can often be documented through titles, liens, account records, or legal agreements.

Whoever controls those keys may effectively control the assets, which means collateral custody cannot be treated as an operational afterthought.

Borrowers need to understand where assets are held, who controls them, whether they can be moved or lent elsewhere, and what safeguards exist between the collateral and the lender's other business activities.

The market has consequently begun moving toward more institutional custody structures.

For example, platforms such as Arch Lending combine crypto-backed borrowing with third-party digital-asset custody rather than treating collateral simply as assets sitting on the lender's own balance sheet. Arch currently supports borrowing against assets including BTC, ETH, SOL and XRP, with funding available in USD or USDC.

This type of architecture reflects a broader transition taking place across crypto.

As more capital enters the market, infrastructure increasingly matters as much as the asset itself.

Custody also leads to another important distinction: what happens to collateral after it has been deposited.

In some lending models, collateral can be rehypothecated, meaning it may be lent, pledged, or otherwise used elsewhere in the financial system.

That can improve capital efficiency, but it also creates additional layers of counterparty risk.

Crypto markets have already demonstrated how quickly those layers can become problematic when leverage builds across multiple institutions.

For borrowers, this means evaluating a crypto-backed loan requires more than comparing interest rates.

Two loans with similar headline pricing may expose collateral to very different operational and counterparty risks depending on how the assets are held and whether they are reused.

Some newer lending structures explicitly avoid rehypothecation and instead keep collateral segregated with an external custodian. Arch, for example, states that collateral held through its custody arrangement is not rehypothecated.

That does not eliminate market risk, but it separates collateral risk from some of the leverage and counterparty risks that have historically complicated crypto lending.

Stablecoins Create a Bridge Between Two Financial Systems

Stablecoins are another important piece of the infrastructure.

A borrower may hold Bitcoin but need dollar-denominated liquidity.

Historically, moving between those two worlds often meant selling the Bitcoin, transferring proceeds through an exchange or bank, and potentially giving up the original position.

The collateral can remain a digital asset while the loan proceeds are distributed in a dollar-linked digital asset such as USDC. The borrower can then use that liquidity inside the crypto ecosystem or convert it into traditional dollars when necessary.

This creates a hybrid financial structure:

None of those components needs to replace the others.

The early cryptocurrency debate often framed blockchain technology and traditional finance as opposing systems.

Either financial services would become decentralized, or established financial institutions would eventually absorb crypto into conventional structures.

The market increasingly suggests a third outcome.

Tokenized assets still require legal ownership structures.

Institutional crypto trading still requires custody and risk controls.

Stablecoins use blockchain settlement while representing traditional currencies.

Crypto-backed lending uses digital collateral while borrowing heavily from long-established principles of secured credit.

This hybrid approach may ultimately prove more important than attempts to reproduce every financial service entirely on-chain.

The strongest technology often disappears into the product.

Users eventually stop caring which database, settlement rail, custody architecture, or risk engine makes a transaction possible. They care whether the financial product works reliably.

Crypto lending may be moving in that direction.

There is a larger implication behind all of this.

A financial asset becomes more useful as the infrastructure around it expands.

Stocks are not valuable only because they can be bought and sold. They can be held in retirement accounts, pledged against credit lines, lent to market participants, used in derivatives, and incorporated into sophisticated portfolio strategies.

Real estate can generate income, secure financing, and serve as collateral for additional investment.

Bitcoin and other digital assets have historically had a much narrower financial lifecycle.

As custody, collateral management, underwriting, and settlement infrastructure improve, crypto can increasingly function as an asset that is not merely owned but financed.

Crypto prices can decline rapidly. Borrowers can face margin requirements or liquidation when collateral values fall. Custody structures and lender terms vary significantly. Borrowing against an appreciating asset can also amplify financial mistakes when leverage is poorly managed.

But they are increasingly the kinds of risks associated with a developing financial market rather than evidence that such a market cannot exist.

The important development is that the infrastructure is becoming sophisticated enough to manage those risks more deliberately.

The most consequential crypto products of the next decade may not feel particularly revolutionary.

They may simply make financial activities that already exist work with a new class of assets.

Borrowing against business assets is normal.

As digital assets become more deeply integrated into portfolios and balance sheets, borrowing against them may eventually seem equally routine.

That transition depends less on speculation and more on infrastructure: custody, collateral management, liquidity, risk controls, and reliable settlement.

And that may ultimately matter more for crypto's long-term financial role than another cycle of new tokens, trading platforms, or speculative applications.

#9581. 5 Tripsy Alternatives for Android in 2026, Including the One I Built

Posted on Nov 2 • Originally published at nomadswipe.com

I built NomadSwipe, an Android app for choosing places in a city. Tripsy is a trip planner for Apple devices, and its Android page says there is no native Android app yet. This comparison covers five apps that run on Android, mine included, and says where Tripsy is the better fit.

Tripsy organises the trip you have already booked. NomadSwipe helps you decide what to do once you land.

Disclosure: I built NomadSwipe, which is Android only. It is one of the five apps compared. Facts come from each app's own website or Google Play listing, read on 2 November 2026. A price appears only where the page we read states one.

AI-assisted: I drafted this article with AI help, then checked each fact against the pages it cites before publishing.

People who search for a Tripsy alternative usually have an Android phone, or travel with someone who does. The table gives the short version. The sections after it cover each app.

Tripsy's home page says you can "instantly turn your reservation emails into a complete trip". Forward an email and the flights, stays and activities are added. It also lists flight alerts for delays, gates and baggage, expenses in any currency, and space for reservations, notes, photos, links and documents.

Its free plan covers unlimited trips, cloud sync, unlimited guests and flight search. Pro adds forwarded reservations, smart import from files, links and text, expenses, flight alerts, a calendar feed and documents. It costs $59 for one year or $299 as a one-time purchase.

The platform is the reason to look elsewhere. Tripsy's Android page offers a waitlist instead of an app. On Android you can view a trip at my.tripsy.app, but editing happens in the Tripsy app.

NomadSwipe solves the other half of the trip. Tripsy organises what you have already booked. NomadSwipe helps you decide what to see once you are there. You open a city and get a deck of real places, one card at a time: swipe right to save, left to skip. Each card shows the category, rating, distance and whether the place is open now. Every saved place lands on a map for that trip, and the list sorts by rating, distance or A to Z.

The free plan includes 3 trips, 2 searched places saved to a trip a month, 2 custom pins a month and a daily limit on saves. Premium comes as Monthly or Lifetime, and up to 20 saved trips are available offline.

The Lisbon sample trip as a list: 16 places, all picked by swiping.

What you gain by moving to NomadSwipe: a way to fill the empty days of a trip on Android. What you give up: email import, flight alerts, expenses and documents. Moving is manual in both directions, because neither app imports the other's trips in the pages we read.

TripIt's Google Play listing says you forward confirmation emails to plans@tripit.com and it builds the itinerary. It says you can share plans with anyone you choose, and find them "even when you're offline". The listing shows 5M+ downloads and an update on 15 October 2026. Its Pro page offers a free 30-day trial, then $49 for a year.

Wanderlog's Google Play listing calls it a "completely free travel app". It says you can add bookings by forwarding emails or connecting Gmail, and that friends can edit the plan in real time. It marks "Access your trip plans offline (Pro)". The listing shows 1M+ downloads.

Tripomatic, formerly Sygic Travel, says on its home page that the free plan has no time limit. It allows up to 5 days with planned activities per calendar month and up to 25 places and hotels per trip, and it shows ads. Its Premium page lists "Free for 7 days, then $29.99/year" and puts offline maps in Premium. It runs on web, Android and Mac.

KDE Itinerary's official page says it "automatically extracts booking data from various input formats". It can find reservations in your email, and it does this locally on your device. It is licensed LGPL-2.0-or-later and lists Android, Plasma Mobile and Linux. Its Play listing shows 5K+ downloads.

We read each app's website and Google Play listing on 2 November 2026, and recorded only what those pages state. Tripsy's facts come from its own website and pricing page. The sample is small, five Android apps plus Tripsy, so treat this as a snapshot, not a market study.

Is there a Tripsy app for Android? No. Tripsy's Android page says there is no native Android app yet and offers a waitlist. You can view a trip in a browser at my.tripsy.app, but you cannot edit it there.

Which Android app is most like Tripsy? For forwarding reservation emails into one itinerary, TripIt is the closest, with KDE Itinerary as the on-device option. Wanderlog also takes forwarded emails or a Gmail connection.

How much does Tripsy cost? Its free plan covers unlimited trips, cloud sync, unlimited guests and flight search. Its pricing page lists Pro at $59 for one year or $299 as a one-time purchase.

Does NomadSwipe import reservation emails like Tripsy? No. NomadSwipe is for choosing places in a city by swiping and seeing them on a map. Use it next to an itinerary app if you need bookings in one place.

Bookings sorted, days still empty? Try NomadSwipe on Google Play. It is Android only.

Prices and features change, so check each app's current page before you buy. Full comparison with sources: 5 Tripsy alternatives on nomadswipe.com.

#9580. NyxJ 2.0: A Pure C11 JSON Engine and Micro-Service Framework

NyxJ is not just a parser: it is an architecture for silence and speed in a world saturated with data. As we approach the release of version 2.0, I want to share what the project delivers: a high-performance JSON engine and micro-service framework written in pure C11, targeting embedded systems, system tools, edge computing, and high-concurrency services.

The design is built around a single static library with no runtime dependencies, native builds for Linux, macOS, and Windows, and a WebAssembly build of the core. The parser is thread-safe and RFC 8259 compliant, with full escape and UTF-8 validation, SIMD scanning (SSE2 / NEON), and line and column information on every error. Security features include JSON DoS protection, the Guardian sanitizer, a Safe-Gate reverse proxy, and HTTPS/TLS.

Productivity tools include dot-path getters, a builder API, JSON-to-struct mapping, a C struct code generator, JSON Schema validation, and JSONPath queries. Performance features include a zero-copy token view, a constant-memory streaming (SAX) parser, an arena allocator, a worker thread pool, and MessagePack support. Data tools cover JSON Patch and Merge Patch diffing, heuristic repair of almost-JSON, and structural checksums.

The framework provides an Express-style router with :params, middleware, async handlers, OpenAPI and Swagger UI generation, and a native HTTP client. Operations features include Prometheus metrics, health and readiness probes with scale hints, heartbeat, Eco-Throttle, and structured logs. The platform layer includes an embedded key-value store with TTL and snapshots, plugins, Unix sockets and shared memory IPC, and gossip clustering. Reliability is addressed through shadow execution and triple modular redundancy with majority vote.

NyxJ 2.0 delivers the bulk of the original roadmap. The sources are released under the Fordima Public License (FPL) v1.0, free for individuals, education, and companies, including embedding in commercial products, with restrictions on building competing engines or offering paid hosted versions. The repository is at https://github.com/fomadev/nyxj. Contributions are welcome under Conventional Commits.

#9579. Trace-X, image forensics

I Built TRACE-X: Exploring Digital Image Forensics Beyond Basic Tampering Detection Images are shared across social media, messaging platforms, and websites every day. But what happens to forensic evidence when an image gets compressed, resized, cropped, or edited before being shared? That's the question that led me to build TRACE-X 2.0 — Transformation-Resilient Adaptive Cross-platform Evidence Engine.

Traditional image-forensics techniques can become less reliable when images undergo common transformations. A forensic signal that is visible in an original image might weaken or change after JPEG compression, resizing, or cropping. I wanted to explore whether combining multiple forensic signals could provide more useful evidence under these conditions.

TRACE-X is an experimental digital image-forensics framework that combines multiple image-analysis techniques into a single evidence-fusion pipeline. Currently, it explores four forensic signals: Error Level Analysis (ELA): Examines differences introduced by JPEG recompression. Discrete Cosine Transform (DCT): Analyses frequency-domain characteristics. Noise Residual Analysis: Examines residual patterns after image smoothing. JPEG Grid Analysis: Examines discontinuities around JPEG block boundaries. These signals are combined using a heuristic, profile-conditioned fusion mechanism. The system generates: Combined evidence maps. Evidence overlays. Exploratory threshold masks. Signal disagreement visualisations. Machine-readable JSON reports. Human-readable HTML reports.

I also implemented experiments involving: JPEG compression at different quality levels. Image resizing. Cropping. Gaussian blur. The objective is to understand how different forensic signals behave when the same image undergoes these transformations.

Python NumPy OpenCV Pillow SciPy Matplotlib Streamlit Pytest

TRACE-X is still an experimental research project. My next goals are: Integrate established image-forensics datasets. Evaluate localisation using ground-truth manipulation masks. Compare against existing forensic baselines. Explore learned transformation profiling. Develop and validate adaptive evidence fusion. Investigate cross-dataset generalisation. I am particularly interested in understanding whether transformation-aware evidence fusion can improve the localisation of manipulations compared with fixed forensic approaches.

GitHub: https://github.com/sreevatsarajesh/Trace-X

I welcome feedback, suggestions, research references, and contributions from anyone working in computer vision, cybersecurity, or digital forensics. If you've worked on image manipulation detection or forensic localisation, I'd love to hear your thoughts. Building, testing, learning, and improving. 🚀

#9577. Inside the OTC Spread: How USDT Pricing Actually Works Under the Hood

You send a request to an API. The response returns a price for USDT that is 0.15% away from what your local exchange ticker shows. You might call it a bad rate. An engineer building payment systems calls it a map of operational friction.

That gap between the spot price you see on a screen and the executable price an Over-The-Counter (OTC) desk offers isn't arbitrary. It is calculated. It represents network fees, settlement delays, counterparty risk, and the cost of moving capital across fragmented infrastructure. For software engineers building crypto-payment rails or reconciliation engines, treating the spread as a simple margin error means misunderstanding the system entirely.

Let's break down how desks usually construct these prices, looking at liquidity, transport layers, and the technical reality of reconciling it all in code.

Retail trading interfaces generally present liquidity as a single order book. OTC desks operate differently. They view liquidity as a distributed graph. A desk might hold inventory on multiple chains simultaneously—Ethereum, Tron, Solana, Polygon—while also maintaining fiat balances in various jurisdictions.

When you request a quote for USDT, the desk's pricing engine doesn't just check one balance. It evaluates the cost of sourcing that specific stablecoin on the specific chain you requested, at that exact moment. If their Tron reserves are low but their Ethereum reserves are high, the quoted price for TRC-20 USDT will likely widen to account for the cost of rebalancing their inventory.

This rebalancing takes time. During that window, the desk carries exposure to market volatility. Even with a stablecoin like USDT, which usually maintains a tight peg to the dollar, slight deviations occur during periods of high network congestion or sudden market stress. The spread absorbs this variance. As a rule, the less liquid the specific chain-to-fiat corridor, the wider the spread needs to be to protect the desk's operating capital.

Engineers understand that moving data has latency costs. Moving money has similar constraints, plus financial overhead. The "rails" refer to both the blockchain networks used for the digital asset and the traditional banking systems used for the fiat leg of the transaction.

Settling a trade via a SWIFT wire transfer usually takes one to three business days. During those days, the capital is locked. The desk factors the opportunity cost of that locked capital into the spread. Conversely, settling via a faster domestic payment rail (like SEPA Instant or FedNow, where supported) might reduce the time-risk, but those rails often carry their own fixed transaction fees.

On the crypto side, gas fees dictate routing logic. If the Ethereum mempool is congested, executing a transfer might cost significantly more than usual. Pricing engines query node RPC endpoints to estimate current base fees and priority tips. This data directly influences the final quote.

Here is a simplified example of how a pricing service might structure a quote object, pulling in rail-specific variables before returning a payload to a client:

Notice the expires_at field. Because gas prices and liquidity shift constantly, quotes are ephemeral. A pricing engine typically invalidates these objects every few seconds. If your application attempts to execute against an expired quote ID, the API will reject the call. Handling this state gracefully in your frontend or backend worker queue is a standard requirement when integrating with institutional desks.

Software engineers tend to think in deterministic terms: if X, then Y. Financial systems are probabilistic. OTC desks price in the probability that something goes wrong.

Counterparty risk is a major variable. If a new corporate client requests a large block of USDT without an established settlement history, the desk's risk management policies—which change frequently based on internal compliance reviews—might automatically widen the spread. This isn't a penalty; it is an insurance premium against the possibility of a failed wire, a frozen bank account, or a disputed transaction.

Regulatory friction adds another layer. Moving fiat across borders involves correspondent banks, each with their own compliance checks. A payment route that touches three intermediary banks will inherently carry more risk of delay or rejection than a direct domestic transfer. The pricing algorithms weigh these routes. Sometimes, a slightly more expensive rail is chosen because it offers higher settlement certainty. The desk optimizes for successful completion, not just the lowest theoretical fee.

For stablecoins specifically, de-peg risk is modeled. While USDT historically stays very close to $1.00, brief fluctuations happen. Desks monitor oracle feeds and secondary market spreads continuously. If the broader market shows signs of stress, the automated spread widens to prevent the desk from selling inventory below its actual replacement cost.

Quoting a price is only half the system. Reconciling the executed trade is where most integration headaches occur. When your application interacts with an OTC desk—often through platforms like gf-pay.best or direct API integrations—you must reconcile two separate states: the fiat ledger and the blockchain ledger.

Blockchain transactions have finality thresholds. On Bitcoin, you might wait for six confirmations. On Tron, finality is faster but still requires monitoring the block height to ensure no reorganizations occur. Your system cannot simply mark a trade as "settled" the moment the RPC endpoint returns a transaction hash. You must poll or listen for webhooks indicating the required confirmation depth has been reached.

Furthermore, floating-point math is dangerous here. Engineers should handle all currency values as integers (representing the smallest unit, like satoshis or wei) or use dedicated decimal libraries. Standard IEEE 754 floats will introduce rounding errors that cause reconciliation mismatches over thousands of transactions.

A typical reconciliation loop looks like this:

If step 3 and step 5 fall out of sync—say, the crypto arrives but the wire is delayed by a weekend—the spread originally quoted had to account for this exact asymmetry. Your database schema needs to support partial states (CRYPTO_RECEIVED_FIAT_PENDING) without breaking downstream reporting tools.

When designing systems around crypto payments, it is tempting to focus purely on throughput and latency. But OTC pricing teaches us that reliability and accurate state management matter more. A system that processes trades instantly but fails to account for rail-specific costs or confirmation delays will bleed capital through unresolved discrepancies.

The spread is essentially a serialized summary of system complexity. Every basis point represents a real-world constraint—a slow bank, a congested mempool, a compliance check, or a temporary lack of inventory on a specific chain. Understanding this anatomy allows engineers to build better parsers, smarter retry logic, and more resilient payment architectures.

Why do OTC spreads for USDT change so rapidly? Spreads are dynamically calculated based on real-time inputs. Network congestion alters gas fees, available inventory shifts as other clients execute trades, and fiat banking hours open or close. Pricing engines typically recalculate these variables every few seconds, meaning a quote generated at 10:00:00 AM might be invalid by 10:00:15 AM.

Can I bypass the spread by using smart contracts directly? Smart contracts automate execution, but they don't eliminate operational costs. If you route through a decentralized liquidity pool, you still pay network gas fees, face potential slippage if the pool lacks depth, and bear the responsibility of managing your own fiat off-ramps. OTC desks bundle these complexities into a single quoted price, handling the bridging between traditional finance and decentralized networks.

How should my application handle an expired quote error? Your system should treat quote expiration as a standard state, not an exception. Build a retry mechanism that automatically requests a fresh quote via the API if the previous one expires before user confirmation or execution. Ensure your UI clearly communicates that prices are time-bound, preventing users from attempting to settle trades against stale data.

#9574. Introducing LearnMathApp: An Open Source Math Learning Project Built with Python and Django 🧮

Helping children practice mathematics while creating opportunities for developers to learn, experiment, and contribute.

What if we could combine learning mathematics with the power of open-source software?

That's the idea behind LearnMathApp, an educational project I'm developing as part of ConnectApp, my independent initiative focused on creating open-source applications, sharing knowledge, and exploring new approaches to software development.

LearnMathApp is designed to help children aged 6 to 12 practice essential mathematical skills through interactive exercises, progressive difficulty levels, and timed challenges.

The application is being developed using Python and Django, making it an interesting project for developers who want to explore web development while contributing to education.

The idea is simple: make mathematical practice more interactive, accessible, and engaging.

LearnMathApp focuses on four fundamental operations:

➕ Addition ➖ Subtraction ✖️ Multiplication ➗ Division

The learning experience is designed around a straightforward process:

The goal is to encourage regular practice while allowing children to progress at a suitable pace.

LearnMathApp is an educational practice tool, not a replacement for teachers or classroom instruction.

I chose Python and Django because they provide a practical foundation for building and evolving educational web applications.

Python offers readable syntax and a broad ecosystem, while Django provides a structured framework for developing web applications.

From a software engineering perspective, LearnMathApp offers opportunities to explore:

These challenges make LearnMathApp interesting beyond its educational purpose.

Developing software for children requires more than implementing the correct functionality.

The interface must be understandable, approachable, and easy to navigate.

I also believe accessibility, readable typography, and appropriate feedback should guide the project's evolution.

The objective is to make the experience inviting while keeping children focused on learning.

One of the principles behind ConnectApp is that open-source software should also create opportunities for learning.

LearnMathApp is intended to serve two complementary purposes.

For children and educators, it aims to provide an accessible environment for reinforcing basic mathematical skills.

For students and developers, it offers a real project where they can study Python, explore Django, understand application architecture, and practice collaborative development.

Instead of working only through isolated programming exercises, contributors can explore how different technical components work together to create a useful application.

I strongly believe that educational technology can benefit from an open and collaborative approach.

Open-source projects allow developers to study existing solutions, propose improvements, learn from one another, and adapt software within the terms of its license.

However, openness also comes with responsibility.

Open Source should never mean lower software quality.

Even an educational application needs careful design, reliable logic, appropriate security measures, and ongoing testing.

My goal is to develop the project with these principles in mind as it evolves.

LearnMathApp is an evolving project, and there are many interesting areas where the community could contribute.

Whether you're an experienced Python developer, a student learning Django, or an educator interested in technology, your perspective could be valuable.

You don't need to be an expert to contribute. Curiosity, constructive feedback, and a willingness to learn are great starting points.

LearnMathApp is part of ConnectApp, an independent initiative I created to explore the possibilities of open-source development and responsible software engineering.

You can learn more about the initiative here:

💻 GitHub: https://github.com/ManuelAf-ConnectApp

If you were building an open-source mathematics application for children, which feature would you prioritize: adaptive difficulty, educational feedback, accessibility, or learning progress?

And if you're learning Python or Django, would you be interested in contributing to an educational project like this?

Let's build software that helps people learn, both as users and as developers.

Because sharing code is valuable, but sharing knowledge is even more powerful. 🚀
