#9573. How Timefolk Is Turning Individual Expertise Into Small Group Sessions

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Jon Stojan is a professional writer based in Wisconsin committed to delivering diverse and exceptional content..

Some skills are easier to practise when more than one person is involved. A presentation can benefit from an audience. Language practice becomes more dynamic with several voices in the room. Interview preparation can expose people to different questions and responses.

Timefolk is extending its skills marketplace around that idea. Through Timefolk, Experts can run small group Events built around a specific skill, with several Clients joining the same practical, in-person session.

The format keeps the same basic structure that sits behind the wider marketplace. The skill, city, session fee and number of available places are clear before someone joins.

In the app, Clients can find an Event through Explore and see the date, skill, fixed session fee, city and remaining spots on the Event card. They can then join and pay through the app. The purpose is established before the group comes together rather than being decided once everyone arrives.

An Expert could run a session around interview practice, Business English, presentation skills, SI tools for work or another practical skill they already use. Several Clients can take part in the same session, creating a different format from an individual session while keeping the activity clearly defined.

For Experts, the group model creates another way to share what they know. Instead of running the same type of session individually with several Clients, an Expert can bring a small group together around one skill. The Expert sets the session fee and the number of available places, while Timefolk provides the marketplace and platform infrastructure around the session.

For Clients, the value is not only the possibility of a lower session fee per person. The group itself can become part of the experience. Someone practising a presentation can receive reactions from more than one participant, while a language session can include different speaking partners. A career focused session can give Clients the opportunity to hear how others approach the same challenge.

The Event still remains tied to one defined skill rather than becoming a general gathering. That distinction is important to Timefolk’s wider positioning as a marketplace for practical, in-person sessions with local Experts.

The platform also keeps the same emphasis on structure. Only ID verified members can join an Event, and every Expert and every Client passes a government ID and liveness check before a session. The exact place is provided before the Event, and the venue must be public. Timefolk’s current product material excludes homes, bars and private rooms from the Event format. Timefolk-media-deck

The session begins through an Event code or QR, creating a clear point at which attendance is recorded. Timefolk also states that only people who attended can leave a review. Timefolk-media-deck

Payments are handled through the app, with Clients able to use methods including Apple Pay, Google Pay or a saved card. Timefolk’s broader payment infrastructure uses Stripe. Timefolk-media-deck

The company has also built specific features around the group format. Its current media deck describes a shared Event page, a QR image that Experts can use when promoting the session, a list showing who attended and tools for managing the Event inside the platform. Clients can receive a full refund if an Event is cancelled or if they leave at least 24 hours before it starts. If the time or place changes, the platform provides a window for Clients to leave without charge. Timefolk-media-deck

Those details matter because group sessions create different operational questions from individual sessions. The platform needs to show who has joined, how many places remain, what happens if the venue changes and how attendance is confirmed.

Timefolk is trying to answer those questions inside the product rather than leaving them to informal coordination. That makes Events more than simply an additional format. They show how a skills marketplace can expand without losing the structure that defines the original model.

One Expert can offer a practical skill to several Clients while the purpose, session fee, location and participation rules remain visible from the beginning.

For Timefolk, that creates another way for expertise to move through a city. A practical skill no longer has to be shared with one Client at a time. It can become a small group session built around the same clear outcome.

Timefolk is available through the web, Timefolk on iOS and Timefolk on Android. Instagram: @timefolkinc. Press: hello@timefolk.com.

#9572. Company Handbook RAG: How to Refresh Policies Without Fine-Tuning

TL;DR: Put changing handbook facts in a retrievable index and use the model to explain the retrieved passages. Fine-tuning is useful for stable behavior, tone, and output shape; it is a poor update mechanism for facts such as carrier cutoffs, warehouse procedures, and escalation contacts. For a logistics handbook, rebuild only the chunks affected by an edit, attach revision metadata, and make ingestion idempotent. That keeps corrections live without another training run and gives each answer something it can cite.

The operational invariant is simple: a handbook revision must become searchable exactly once, and an answer must identify the revision it used. I have been paged by missed jobs and duplicate deliveries. That history makes me distrust a design where “the training finished” is the only evidence that a correction took effect. A queue can redeliver. A scheduled run can overlap. The write path has to expect both.

Retrieval does add moving parts: a chunker, an embedding step, an index, and a query path. Those parts are visible and testable, though. Fine-tuning moves the update into a slower training artifact and still does not provide source citations. The original RAG paper describes the useful separation: parametric memory in the model, non-parametric memory in an external index.

Consider a dock supervisor asking, “What is the current procedure for a damaged refrigerated shipment?” The answer may depend on a policy edited this morning. With retrieval, the edited passage is re-chunked and indexed; the next query can retrieve that revision immediately after the indexing write succeeds. With fine-tuning, the old fact remains baked into the model until another training run produces and deploys a replacement.

Fine-tuning is not a defective form of retrieval. It is a different tool. If the company wants every incident summary to follow a durable format, examples used in fine-tuning can teach that behavior. The live emergency phone number should still come from retrieval.

There is also a clean failure boundary. If no eligible passage is retrieved, the system can decline to answer or route the question to an owner. A trained model has no equivalent built-in proof that a particular handbook fact was present in its training data.

Index cost at scale is driven partly by how much text is embedded and rewritten. A naive pipeline that assigns random IDs to every chunk turns a one-line handbook edit into a full set of new records. Stable IDs let the writer upsert the changed content and leave identical chunks alone.

The following program splits a small logistics handbook by paragraph, normalizes whitespace, and derives each ID from the document name, revision, and content. It is deliberately plain. Replace the sample string with text extracted by your existing document parser.

Including the revision in the ID preserves history, which is useful when answers must be auditable. If the index should contain only the current handbook, use a deterministic logical chunk key instead and replace its contents on update. Do not casually combine those policies. Keeping every revision without a query-time “current revision” filter can retrieve withdrawn instructions; overwriting everything destroys the evidence needed for an audit.

Chunk size is not a magic constant. Split on the smallest section that still carries a complete instruction, then measure retrieval quality on real handbook questions. Tables, warnings, and numbered procedures often need different boundaries from prose. More tiny chunks can increase record count and embedding work; giant chunks can return irrelevant text and waste model context. Start with document structure, not a fashionable token count.

Assume at-least-once delivery even if the happy path usually runs once. The job identity should include the handbook, revision, and chunking algorithm version. A worker records completion only after the index acknowledges the write. On retry, it presents the same deterministic chunk IDs, so an upsert replaces the same records instead of multiplying them.

Before implementing that adapter, inspect the provider's current schema instead of copying an old request body from a blog post. The program below makes one real call to Infrai's public discovery surface, authenticates from the environment, sets the HTTP method explicitly, checks error responses, and backs off on HTTP 429 while honoring Retry-After. It prints the discovered definition as JSON, including the schema and runnable examples supplied by that surface. That is the contract to use when implementing the vector upsert adapter; no request fields are guessed here.

Once the adapter is built from that schema, “one logical record after two deliveries” is a property worth putting in a test and a runbook. Track the source revision, chunker version, expected chunk count, acknowledged chunk count, and terminal job state too. Those values answer the first incident question: did the new policy reach the index completely? I first look for a mismatch between expected and acknowledged counts, because a green scheduler only proves that a scheduler fired; it does not prove every chunk became queryable, that an obsolete revision was excluded, or that a retry reused the original IDs. The completion check must cover the result the reader depends on.

Do not acknowledge the queue message before the index write. Do not create a fresh identifier inside a retry loop. These two mistakes turn intermittent failures into either missing facts or duplicate search results.

The products below can all participate in a retrieval system, but they put cost and operational work in different places. I would benchmark them with the same corpus, embedding model, metadata filters, and relevance set. Vendor marketing numbers are not interchangeable measurements.

Infrai's relevant advantage here is integration friction: anything that sends HTTP can call its REST API, with no client library version to maintain. Its discovery surface also exposes request schemas and runnable Go examples, which is useful when implementing an adapter without guessing fields. Keep the adapter anyway. The handbook, revision, chunk ID, and citation contract should belong to your application rather than a provider.

There are real limitations and trade-offs. Infrai is a poor fit when policy requires the vector service to run entirely inside infrastructure your team controls; self-hosted Qdrant, Weaviate, or PostgreSQL with pgvector deserves the first evaluation in that case. If the team already has mature PostgreSQL operations and the handbook corpus fits comfortably within its capacity plan, pgvector may remove a service boundary. Conversely, a team that wants a dedicated managed vector database and its surrounding tooling should compare Pinecone directly. The REST consolidation benefit matters only if consolidation is actually a requirement.

For index cost, measure the whole change cycle: initial embeddings, records retained, bytes of metadata, update frequency, replicas, queries, backup policy, and engineer time for self-hosted systems. Price is not the headline. A design that cheaply stores stale or duplicated chunks has failed its job.

Run a representative test before committing. Use the actual distribution of policy pages, tables, and procedures; replay the same revision twice; edit one paragraph; confirm that only the intended records change; and ask questions whose answers span section boundaries. Record recall and citation correctness alongside resource use. One aggregate relevance score can hide a dangerous miss in a safety procedure.

Retrieval is unnecessary when the application has no changing external facts and the goal is purely behavioral. A classifier with a fixed label set or a formatter with stable examples may benefit from fine-tuning without an index. A tiny handbook with exact identifiers may be better served by ordinary database lookup or full-text search. Vector similarity is not mandatory merely because a model will read the result.

Retrieval also does not guarantee truth. It can fetch the wrong chunk, retrieve an obsolete revision, or pass conflicting policies to the model. Access control must be applied before passages enter the answer context, especially when regional or customer-specific procedures share an index. Evaluate retrieval separately from generation so the team can tell whether a bad answer began with a search miss or with misuse of good evidence.

The final decision is therefore narrower than “RAG versus fine-tuning.” Keep mutable logistics facts in a system that can update, filter, inspect, and cite them. Fine-tune only the stable behavior that deserves to persist across handbook revisions. Then make the ingestion path boring: deterministic chunks, idempotent writes, explicit revisions, and an observable completion check.

#9571. Following the FortiBleed path from VPN access to ransomware

The FortiBleed credential leak became more consequential when investigators linked it to ransomware access. BleepingComputer reported that the FBI described the attack chain as an initial entry point for ransomware affiliates, including INC, Lynx and Payload groups [4]. Earlier reporting connected the credential-theft infrastructure to INC and Lynx operations [5].

Those links do not mean every organization in the dataset was attacked. They do show why a valid FortiGate or VPN credential cannot be treated as a low-severity finding.

A password-authenticated VPN login can look like normal remote work. The attacker may test a credential, wait, return through a different address and establish a session before making significant changes.

The JaCIRT advisory described the risk of lateral movement into Active Directory and other internal systems after access to a FortiGate [1]. The FBI report added that attackers have created administrator accounts and removed legitimate administrative access, making recovery harder [4].

The investigation should establish a timeline from the first suspicious authentication through endpoint, directory and data-access events. Review VPN sessions, administrator logins, firewall configuration changes, domain-controller activity and endpoint logons. Preserve the original logs before rebuilding a device.

An attacker with administrative access can create another account, change authentication settings, add a VPN user or alter a trusted source. These changes can survive the removal of the first credential.

That is why containment must include configuration integrity. Fortinet advised comparing the device against a known-good configuration and checking for unexpected accounts or VPN changes [3]. The review should include logging destinations, routes, certificates and integration settings, not just the account that appears in the credential list.

If the attacker reached Active Directory, the response also needs identity containment. Reset affected credentials, revoke sessions and tokens, review privileged groups and service accounts, and search for new authentication paths. The network edge and the identity system have to be treated as one access chain.

The FortiGate may contain the only record of the initial source address, account, session and configuration change. Export logs and configuration before cleanup when policy allows. Record file hashes and collection times.

Do not overwrite the evidence with a factory reset or a clean configuration. If the device must be replaced, keep the original storage and logs in a controlled state for investigation.

The ZoomEye query app="FortiGate" && port="443" returned 41,734 observations on October 19, 2026 [6]. It can guide a review of externally visible FortiGate services and help identify unmanaged edge devices.

The count does not show ransomware access. It describes product exposure. Use it with authentication and configuration evidence to decide which devices demand immediate containment.

The network, identity and incident-response teams should share one timeline and one asset register. Confirm which sessions were terminated, which accounts were removed, which credentials were rotated and which persistence checks were completed.

The final decision should be based on evidence that the access path is closed and the configuration is understood. A patched firewall with an unknown administrator account is not contained.

#9570. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

#9569. Day 14: I Gave HYNA-Stage a Brain (AI Support + Human Escalation, Built on a $150 Phone) 🧠🤖

It was late at night. I was staring at a glowing terminal in Termux on my $150 Android phone.

I had just finished wiring up the final piece of HYNA-Stage v2.3.0. I typed a test message into the new support chat:

"I'm the official support assistant created by the HYNA-Stage team. I'm here to help you deploy, debug, and scale. Let me show you why HYNA-Stage is the fastest way to spin up an isolated cloud sandbox..."

It defended the product. It knew its name. It held the line.

For a second, I just sat there. I didn't just build a CLI tool anymore. I built a company with a support team.

Welcome to Day 14 of building HYNA-Stage, and the day we went from "sandbox deployer" to "living SaaS platform."

1. The HYNA AI Developer Assistant Powered by Groq's LPU inference engine running a 120B parameter MoE model (openai/gpt-oss-120b), the AI answers user questions instantly through a Supabase Edge Function middleman.

But here's the key: it's not a generic chatbot. I gave it a 7-rule constitutional prompt:

2. HITL (Human-in-the-Loop) Escalation This is the feature that gave me goosebumps.

When the AI encounters a refund request, an unresolvable bug, or an explicit demand for a human, it silently appends a hidden [HUMAN_REVIEW] tag to its response.

The frontend JavaScript intercepts this tag, strips it from the UI so the user never sees it, and writes the ticket to the support_tickets table with needs_human: true.

Suddenly, I had a CEO dashboard. A real queue. A system that knows when the AI should stop talking and a human should step in.

3. Silent Attribution & Referral Engine When a user clicks a tracking link like /go/nicky, the JS extracts the ref parameter, saves it to localStorage, and fires a POST to the referrals table. When they sign up, the system pulls that value and maps it to profiles.referred_by, automating my CMO Nicky's 15% revenue share attribution.

No spreadsheets. No manual math. Just clean, scalable growth infrastructure.

Building a multi-service AI platform on a phone is not easy. Here are the walls I hit:

There were moments today where I genuinely wanted to quit.

I don't have a MacBook. I don't have a dual-monitor setup. I don't have a YC check. I have a 1GB RAM phone, Termux, and a relentless obsession with building HYNAWEB.

But then the AI replied. And it wasn't just a generic ChatGPT response. It was my AI. It defended HYNA-Stage. It held the line. It knew its name.

When I watched the [HUMAN_REVIEW] tag work—when I saw the database light up with needs_human: true—I realized something. I didn't just build a sandbox deployer. I built a company. I built a support team. I built an ecosystem.

The stack is alive. Netlify, Supabase, Cloudflare, E2B, Groq. They are all talking to each other.

This isn't a side project anymore. This is the foundation of HYNAWEB. And I built it from my pocket.

#9568. Sellvia in 2026: The Tech Behind Its Digital Stores, Built-In Ads, and Orders

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Business Developement Manager with a demonstrated history of working in the public relations and communication.

Opening an ecommerce store used to involve several separate projects. A seller needed a website, hosting, product pages, payment tools, marketing software, and a system for keeping track of orders. None of those tasks was impossible, but the number of services involved made a small online business surprisingly complicated to operate.

Sellvia takes a more integrated approach. Instead of asking users to assemble a store from independent services, the platform provides a managed storefront, access to a product catalog, promotional tools, and a dashboard for everyday operations.

That approach is timely. Sellvia appeared at No. 591 on the 2026 Inc. 5000 list of fast-growing private companies in the United States. Beyond the ranking, the more interesting story is how the platform brings several parts of digital commerce into one workflow.

Sellvia is an ecommerce platform that helps users launch an online store and manage its day-to-day operations. Its turnkey store offering is based on WordPress with Sellvia's own plugin and managed hosting.

The company supplies a ready-to-use store structure rather than leaving the owner to configure a server and assemble a large collection of plugins. Product management, store activity, and available marketing tools are reached through the Sellvia Dashboard.

This design changes the work involved in getting started. A new owner can spend more time choosing products, improving descriptions, and planning how to reach customers. They spend less time on hosting arrangements and the technical maintenance of separate systems.

The platform is especially interesting for someone who wants to run a store without becoming a WordPress administrator. Sellvia manages much of the underlying environment, while users work with the controls provided in the dashboard.

One of Sellvia's practical advantages is access to an existing product catalog.

Digital products can include ebooks, downloadable guides, educational material, courses, and templates. Unlike physical merchandise, these products do not require a warehouse or parcel delivery. Customers receive access to digital content after completing the relevant purchase process.

Take a store specializing in productivity and professional development. The owner might organize useful digital resources around planning, career skills, or personal organization. The work becomes selecting coherent offers and presenting them clearly instead of sourcing physical inventory and arranging shipping.

Product quality and relevance still matter. A broad catalog is most useful when the store has a clear audience and a sensible way of helping visitors choose among available products.

This is also why digital commerce is an attractive starting point for an integrated platform: product presentation, customer purchase, and content delivery can be coordinated electronically.

The key to understanding Sellvia is to look beyond the storefront itself.

The storefront is the public-facing part of the business. It presents products, organizes categories, and gives visitors a place to browse.

The product catalog supplies the items the owner can select and publish. This reduces the preparation involved in building a store from an empty website.

Sellvia Ads provides a managed promotional service within Sellvia's ecosystem. Users can review the available promotion settings and activity through their account rather than building the entire advertising workflow from scratch.

Order management brings transaction records and order activity into the dashboard, helping users see which orders need attention and which have progressed through the applicable processing steps.

Reporting connects these activities. Instead of judging the business only by how the homepage looks, users can monitor product activity, promotion, and orders in one working environment.

These functions have different jobs, but they share a practical purpose: reducing the number of disconnected tools a store owner needs to manage.

Marketing is often the next challenge after a store goes live. Having a finished website does not mean that people will automatically discover its products.

Sellvia Ads addresses part of that challenge with a managed promotion service. Its published terms describe promotion through Sellvia-operated digital properties and internal placement systems. Available budgets and service options are managed from the platform environment.

That makes Sellvia Ads different from an ordinary advertising account in which a merchant manually controls every external placement. It is important to understand that the internal promotion service does not necessarily function as a campaign sending visitors directly to the owner's branded website.

For someone new to advertising, a managed service can reduce the number of settings they need to learn at the beginning. It also provides a convenient starting point for examining how promotional activity relates to product demand.

The useful metrics are the ones tied to business decisions: what promotion was used, which products generated activity, and how actual orders compare with promotional spending. Advertised exposure is not the same as a completed order, and keeping those measurements separate leads to better decisions.

The digital-order journey is short enough to understand without technical jargon.

First, a product is selected from the catalog and presented to customers through the relevant store or sales interface. The product page should explain what the buyer receives and make the offer easy to evaluate.

Next, the customer completes the checkout process available for that purchase. The precise payment flow depends on the store's configured arrangement.

Once the purchase has been processed, the buyer can receive access to the digital material through the applicable delivery process. The order is also recorded in the systems used to manage store activity.

These steps show the practical value of selling downloadable resources: there is no shipping label, carrier pickup, or warehouse dispatch between a completed digital purchase and access to the purchased material.

The store owner should still test the experience personally. Product pages, checkout instructions, access links, and order records should be clear and consistent, particularly on mobile devices.

A useful ecommerce dashboard should support decisions, not merely display numbers.

Sellvia groups important store functions in a central workspace. Users can work with the catalog, review order information, access available promotional controls, and inspect reporting provided for their account.

For example, an owner who has added several digital guides can check whether visitors are engaging with those offers and whether the products are generating orders. When experimenting with promotion, the same owner can compare activity over time and decide which subjects deserve more attention.

Centralization matters because small operational tasks accumulate. Every additional service normally introduces another login, another set of settings, and another place where data might need to be checked. A connected dashboard reduces that fragmentation.

For additional explanations of the interface and individual features, Sellvia.info provides platform-focused guides and resources.

Sellvia's published September 2026 terms describe three base subscription levels:

The standard introductory offer described in those terms includes a 14-day trial. The availability of higher tiers and promotional offers may be subject to additional conditions.

The base subscription covers the relevant store infrastructure and platform access. Services such as advertising and certain order-related operations can have separate charges, so the subscription amount should not be mistaken for the total cost of operating a store.

A sensible first budget separates recurring software costs from optional promotion. That makes it much easier to test the platform methodically and understand the economics of a specific product category.

Before investing heavily in advertising, run through the service as both a store owner and a customer.

Review the catalog and select products that fit a recognizable audience. Check that each description makes the content and intended buyer clear. Open the storefront on a phone and make sure the navigation and product pages are readable.

Then inspect the purchase path that applies to your configuration, including what happens after checkout and how buyers obtain their digital content.

Finally, review the dashboard's order and promotion tools. Identify the information that will help you compare products and measure spending. These simple checks reveal much more about everyday usability than a feature list alone.

This kind of evaluation is also a useful way to understand the platform's central benefit: the work of running a digital store is organized around one connected operating environment.

Sellvia's model reflects a wider change in ecommerce software. Increasingly, the appeal of a platform is not just how quickly it creates a website but how much routine operational work it brings together afterward.

A hosted store, existing product catalog, built-in promotion, order management, and accessible reporting each solve a different problem. Their combined value is that owners spend less time coordinating software and more time understanding products and customers.

That does not replace sound business decisions. Choosing useful products, describing them accurately, managing expenses, and serving customers still matter.

But for someone who wants a practical way to begin selling digital products, Sellvia provides an integrated starting point. Its 2026 ecosystem shows how the storefront has become one component of a broader digital-commerce workspace.

#9566. Butter Scraped Over Too Much Bread

Everyone I know is tired. Not "I stayed up too late" tired. The other kind. The kind where you open your laptop on Monday and it feels like Thursday.

I keep thinking about Bilbo Baggins. Early in The Fellowship of the Ring, right before he walks out of the Shire, he tells Gandalf he feels thin and stretched,"like butter that has been scraped over too much bread."

I first read that as a kid and thought it was a funny line about breakfast. I now read it as the most accurate description of modern knowledge work ever written. Tolkien was an Oxford professor. He knew.

Growth is never enough A lot of companies I know are growing fast. Double digits, year over year. By any sane measure, that's a great business. People write case studies about less. It still feels like we're losing.

Here's the math as it lands on a human being. Every one of us is allocated at 100%. Forty hours a week, all billable, all customer projects. No slack. No buffer. No time set aside for learning, which is a strange choice in a field that reinvents itself every six months.

Growth doesn't buy breathing room. It buys more bread. The butter stays the same size. (I have checked. The butter has not grown)

We would never do this to a server Nobody reading dev.to would run a production database at 100% CPU and call it efficient. We'd call it an incident.

Queueing theory explains why. Take the simplest model: one server, jobs arriving at random. Queueing people call it M/M/1. In that model, the time a job spends in the system grows with 1 / (1 − utilization). At 50% busy, a job takes twice as long as the work itself. At 90%, ten times as long. At 99%, a hundred. It doesn’t grow politely. It goes vertical.

People are not M/M/1 queues. we're worse. I'm aware. I have been asked to stop saying "throughput" at dinner. But the shape holds. At 100% allocation, every surprise becomes a backlog. A sick kid. A customer escalation. A production bug at 4:55 on a Friday. There is no capacity to absorb any of it, so it gets absorbed by evenings and weekends instead.

We give our EC2 fleets headroom. We set autoscaling at 70%. We know that a system with zero spare capacity isn't efficient. It's fragile. Then we staff our teams like we've never heard of any of this.

Someone will point out that GenAI makes everything faster. More butter! I use these tools every day. They are fast. But look at the math again. Utilization is work coming in divided by work getting done. Double the speed, double the incoming work, and you’re right back at 100%. Faster servers don’t fix a queue if you just feed them faster. Economists call this the Jevon Paradox1. When steam engines got more efficient, Britain didn’t burn less coal. It burned more. AI can absolutely be more butter. But if every hour it saves becomes another project, we haven’t fixed anything. We’ve just bought a bigger loaf.

Zero learning time is technical debt with a pulse The part that bothers me most isn't the hours. It's the zero. Zero hours for learning means the only way to learn is on the customer's dime or on your own time. Neither scales. The first is risky. The second is how you get a team of people reading re:Invent announcements at 11 p.m. with one eye open.

We all understand technical debt. You skip the refactor to hit the date, and you pay interest later. Skipping learning works the same way. Except the interest compounds in people. Skills go stale. Curiosity goes quiet. The engineers who could have figured out the next big thing are too busy shipping the last one. And then, one day, a very good person updates their LinkedIn. That's the payment coming due.

More butter, or less bread There are only two fixes. Get more butter, or spread it over less bread. Some ideas, none of them new, all of them ignored:

Plan for 80%, not 100%. The missing 20% isn't waste. It's the headroom that absorbs surprises, so surprises don't eat people. Put learning on the schedule. Four hours a week, protected, not "whenever you find time."

Nobody finds time. Time is not under the couch.

Count recovery as capacity. A rested engineer does in one hour what a burned-out one does in three. That's not soft. That's arithmetic. Hire ahead of the curve. If you're growing fast, staffing to last year's demand guarantees everyone is stretched this year.

Bilbo, notably, did not optimize his butter. He didn't install a better toaster or adopt a new bread framework. He left. He went to Rivendell, sat by the fire, and wrote a book. Most of us can't run off with the elves. But we can stop pretending that a team at 100% is a team at its best. It isn't. It's a team one bad week away from breaking.

If everyone you know is running on fumes too, you're not imagining it. And it's not a personal failing. It's a capacity problem. Those, at least, we know how to solve. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jevons_paradox

#9565. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

#9564. 4 Wonderful Signs You Have A High IQ

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Four things that indicate high intelligence in a person.

Being open to experience, cooperative, happy and having strong perceptual skills are all signs that you have a high IQ, psychological research finds.

Of these, being open to experience is a particularly strong sign…

Insatiable curiosity, an active fantasy life, a sensitivity to emotions and an appreciation of art and beauty are all linked to high IQ.

These are all aspects of the major personality trait called ‘openness to experience’.

People who are open to experience are more interested in things that are complex, new and unconventional.

Being open to experience is so powerful that it is linked to intelligence when measured almost 40 years later.

Children who scored higher on IQ tests at just 11-years-old were more open to experience when they were 50-years-old, the psychologists found.

Intelligent people are better at cooperating with others.

While personality traits like being generous and conscientious have an effect on cooperation, higher IQ is the main factor that encourages people to work well together.

People with higher intelligence use more consistent strategies and consider the consequences of their actions.

That is why people with high IQs are so essential: without them society would not work.

The finding goes against the popular idea that being intelligent somehow predisposes people to unhappiness.

The study looked at happiness in the best-known sense of feeling positive emotions and being satisfied with your life.

The results showed that people with the lowest IQ (70 – 99) were the least happy in comparison to those with the highest IQs (120 – 129).

People with high IQs have stronger basic perceptual skills, research finds.

For example, they can tell which way objects are moving more quickly.

They are also better at blocking out background information to make their judgement.

Imagine a ball thrown at high speed — a more intelligent person can pick up its trajectory faster.

A higher IQ makes the brain faster at a fundamental level.

It helps underline that high IQ is about more than just solving puzzles or making the ‘right’ decision.

#9563. Your fingerprint prompt is a speed bump, not a lock: Android biometrics with a CryptoObject

Posted on Nov 2 • Originally published at chartmann1590.github.io

A fingerprint prompt feels like security. The user touches the sensor, a little animation plays, the app opens. But look at what most implementations do with the result: onAuthenticationSucceeded() sets a boolean, and the boolean opens the screen. Anyone who can change that boolean, with a debugger on a rooted phone or by patching the APK, opens the screen without a fingerprint. Worse, the data behind the screen was never protected at all; it was sitting in storage the whole time.

A biometric check is only as strong as what it unlocks. This post shows the difference between a prompt that decides a branch in your code and a prompt that releases a cryptographic key, and how to build the second kind with androidx.biometric.

Use the Jetpack Biometric library rather than the platform BiometricPrompt directly. It works back to older Android versions, handles device differences and gives you one API.

1.1.0 is the stable release in October 2026. The 1.4.0 alpha line adds an activity-result API, a biometric-compose artifact and KeyAgreement support in CryptoObject; everything below uses the stable BiometricPrompt API, which the alpha keeps.

BiometricManager.Authenticators defines three types, and the difference between the first two is the whole story:

The device maker decides which sensor is Class 2 or Class 3, not you. Many face unlock implementations are Class 2 and many fingerprint sensors are Class 3, but do not assume; ask the system.

A few rules from the documentation shape everything:

Call canAuthenticate() with exactly the combination you will pass to the prompt:

When nothing is enrolled, on Android 11 (API level 30) and higher you can send the user to Settings.ACTION_BIOMETRIC_ENROLL, passing the authenticators you accept in Settings.EXTRA_BIOMETRIC_AUTHENTICATORS_ALLOWED. When biometrics are unavailable, fall back to your normal sign-in rather than hiding the feature.

The common version calls showNotes() from onAuthenticationSucceeded(). A successful callback proves only that the system said the user passed, and your code then trusts a callback inside your own process. With a patched APK, or on a device where an attacker controls your process, that callback can be faked, and the notes were readable all along. It is fine for confirming that the person holding an already-unlocked phone is probably the owner before showing something mildly sensitive. It is not a lock.

The fix is to make the prompt release something the app cannot get any other way. Create a key in the Android Keystore that can only be used after a strong biometric check, and encrypt the sensitive data with it. Now the only way to decrypt is to pass the prompt, because the Keystore enforces the check outside your process, often in secure hardware.

Initialize a Cipher with the key, wrap it in a CryptoObject and pass it to authenticate(). On success, the cipher in the result is authorized for one operation:

Decryption is the same with Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE and a GCMParameterSpec(128, blob.iv). Store the IV next to the ciphertext; it is not secret, but GCM needs it, and the Keystore generates a fresh random IV for each encryption by default.

When the user adds a new fingerprint or removes the screen lock, the key is gone for good and cipher.init() throws KeyPermanentlyInvalidatedException. That is the system doing its job. Catch it, delete the key alias and the ciphertext it protected, and ask the user to sign in again the normal way. Never treat it as a crash:

Good uses: unlocking a stored refresh token so a returning user signs in with a fingerprint; confirming a sensitive action such as deleting the account, where the strongest version signs a server nonce with a biometric-bound private key; and a private vault inside the app with its own authentication-bound key.

Bad uses: a prompt in front of the whole app while the data sits unencrypted behind it, or a prompt treated as a replacement for server-side authentication. After too many failed attempts the system locks biometrics out and reports it through onAuthenticationError(); offer the screen lock or your normal sign-in instead of looping the prompt. And if what you want is "sign in with my fingerprint", passkeys are the better answer, since the credential provider already uses the screen lock and biometrics.

This is adapted from my book Sign-In and Security Done Right (Android the Right Way, Book 9). The free sample is here and the full book is here.

#9562. Top 10 AI Tools in 2023 That Will Make Your Life Easier



 In this article, we explore the top 10 AI tools that are driving innovation and efficiency in various industries. These tools are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The tools included in our list are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for a variety of applications. Some of the tools focus on natural language processing, such as ChatGPT and Grammarly, while others focus on image and video generation, such as DALL-E and Lumen5. Other tools such as OpenAI Codex, Tabnine, Canva, Jasper AI,, and Surfer SEO are designed to help with specific tasks such as code understanding content writing and website optimization. This list is a great starting point for anyone looking to explore the possibilities of AI and how it can be applied to their business or project.

So let’s dive into

1. ChatGPT

ChatGPT is a large language model that generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts. It can be used for tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion. It can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing, and generates coherent and fluent text, but should be used with care as it may generate text that is biased, offensive, or factually incorrect.

Pros:

  • Generates human-like responses to a variety of prompts
  • Can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as language translation, question answering, and text completion
  • Can handle a wide range of topics and styles of writing
  • Can generate coherent and fluent text, even when completing a given text prompt.

Cons:

  • May generate text that is biased or offensive
  • Can generate text that is not accurate or factually correct
  • May require large amounts of computational resources to run
  • The model can sometimes generate text that is not coherent or fluent, depending on the prompt given.

Overall, ChatGPT is a powerful tool for natural language processing, but it should be used with care and with an understanding of its limitations.

2. DALL-E

DALL-E is a generative model developed by OpenAI that is capable of generating images from text prompts. It is based on the GPT-3 architecture, which is a transformer-based neural network language model that has been trained on a massive dataset of text. DALL-E can generate images that are similar to a training dataset and it can generate high-resolution images that are suitable for commercial use.

Pros:

  • Generates high-resolution images
  • Can generate images from text prompts
  • It can be fine-tuned for specific tasks such as generating images of a certain style or category

Cons:

  • May generate images that are not entirely original and could be influenced by the training data
  • May require significant computational resources to run
  • The quality of the generated images may vary depending on the specific prompt

Overall, DALL-E is a powerful AI-based tool for generating images, it can be used for a variety of applications such as creating images for commercial use, gaming, and other creative projects. It is important to note that the generated images should be reviewed and used with care, as they may not be entirely original and could be influenced by the training data.

3. Lumen5

Lumen5 is a content creation platform that uses AI to help users create videos, social media posts, and other types of content. It has several features that make it useful for content creation and marketing, including:

Pros:

  • Automatically summarizes text from a blog post, article, or another source into a script for a video or social media post
  • Offers a library of royalty-free videos, images, and music to use in content
  • Has a drag-and-drop interface for easy content creation
  • Can create videos in multiple languages
  • Has a built-in analytics tool to track the performance of created content.

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material
  • The automatic summarization feature may not always capture the main points of the source material
  • The library of videos, images, and music is limited.
  • The analytics feature is basic

Overall, Lumen5 is a useful tool for creating content quickly and easily, it can help automate the process of creating videos, social media posts, and other types of content. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the source material and it is important to review and edit the content before publishing it.

4. Grammarly

Grammarly is a writing-enhancement platform that uses AI to check for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text. It also provides suggestions for improving the clarity, concision, and readability of the text. It has several features that make it useful for improving writing, including:

Pros:

  • Checks for grammar, punctuation, and spelling errors in the text
  • Provides suggestions for improving clarity, concision, and readability
  • Can be integrated with various apps and platforms such as Microsoft Office, Google Docs, and social media platforms
  • Offers a browser extension and a desktop app
  • Has a premium version with more advanced features such as plagiarism detection and more

Cons:

  • The suggestions provided may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The grammar checker may not always recognize context-specific language use
  • The free version has limited features
  • Limited to English language only
  • Overall, Grammarly is a useful tool for improving writing, it can help users identify and correct grammar and punctuation errors, and improve the clarity, concision, and readability of their text. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate.

5.OpenAI Codex

OpenAI Codex is a system developed by OpenAI that can create code from natural language descriptions of software tasks. The system is based on the GPT-3 model and can generate code in multiple programming languages.

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of writing code
  • Can help developers to be more productive
  • Can help non-technical people to create software
  • Can generate code in multiple programming languages

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description
  • The generated code may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex software tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, OpenAI Codex is a powerful tool that can help automate the process of writing code and make it more accessible to non-technical people. However, the quality of the generated code may vary depending on the task description and it is important to review and test the code before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

6. Tabnine

Tabnine is a code completion tool that uses AI to predict and suggest code snippets. It is compatible with multiple programming languages and can be integrated with various code editors.

Pros:

  • Can improve coding efficiency by suggesting code snippets based on context
  • Can complete entire code blocks
  • Can predict variables, functions, and other elements of code
  • Can be integrated with various code editors

Cons:

  • The suggestions may not always be accurate or appropriate
  • The system may not always be able to understand the context of the code
  • May not work with all code editors
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the code.

Overall, TabNine is a useful tool for developers that can help improve coding efficiency and reduce the time spent on writing code. However, it is important to review the suggestions provided by the tool and use them with caution, as they may not always be accurate or appropriate. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the developer's knowledge.

7. Jasper AI

Jasper is a content writing and content generation tool that uses artificial intelligence to identify the best words and sentences for your writing style and medium in the most efficient, quick, and accessible way.

Pros:

  • User-friendly interface
  • Generates a wide variety of content types
  • Guarantees 100% unique and free-plagiarism content
  • SEO friendly
  •  Create articles of up to 10k words

Cons:

  • Not the cheapest AI writer on the market

8. Surfer SEO

Surfer SEO is a software tool designed to help website owners and digital marketers improve their search engine optimization (SEO) efforts. The tool provides a variety of features that can be used to analyze a website's on-page SEO, including:

Features:

  • A site audit tool that checks for technical SEO issues
  • A content editor that suggests optimizations for individual pages
  • A keyword research tool that suggests keywords to target
  • A SERP analyzer that shows how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • A backlink analysis tool that shows the backlinks pointing to a website.

Pros:

  • Can help website owners and marketers identify technical SEO issues
  • Can provide suggestions for optimizing individual pages
  • Can help with keyword research
  • Can show how a website's pages rank for specific keywords
  • Can provide insight into a website's backlink profile

Cons:

  • Some features may require a paid subscription
  • The tool is not a guarantee of better ranking
  • The tool can only analyze the data it has access to
  • The tool's suggestions may not always be applicable or optimal

Overall, Surfer SEO can be a useful tool for website owners and digital marketers looking to improve their SEO efforts. However, it is important to remember that it is just a tool and should be used in conjunction with other SEO best practices. Additionally, the tool is not a guarantee of better ranking.

9. Zapier

Zapier is a web automation tool that allows users to automate repetitive tasks by connecting different web applications together. It does this by creating "Zaps" that automatically move data between apps, and can also be used to trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Features:

  • Can connect over 3,000 web applications
  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can create "Zaps" to move data between apps
  • Can trigger certain actions in one app based on events in another app.

Pros:

  • Can automate repetitive tasks
  • Can save time
  • Can improve workflow
  • Can increase productivity
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of web applications

Cons:

  • Can be difficult to set up
  • May require some technical skills
  • May require a paid subscription for some features
  • Some apps may not be compatible
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the apps

Overall, Zapier is a useful tool that can help users automate repetitive tasks and improve workflow. It can save time and increase productivity by connecting different web applications together. However, it may require some technical skills and some features may require a paid subscription. It is important to use the tool with caution and not to rely too much on it, to understand the apps better.

10. Compose AI

Compose AI is a company that specializes in developing natural language generation (NLG) software. Their software uses AI to automatically generate written or spoken text from structured data, such as spreadsheets, databases, or APIs.

Features:

  • Automatically generates written or spoken text from structured data
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources
  • Can be used for a variety of applications such as creating reports, summaries, and explanations
  • Provides an API and a user-friendly interface

Pros:

  • Can automate the process of creating written or spoken content
  • Can help users create more accurate and consistent content
  • Can help users save time by automating repetitive tasks
  • Can be integrated with a wide range of data sources

Cons:

  • The quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source
  • The generated content may not always be optimal or efficient
  • The system may not be able to handle complex tasks
  • Dependence on the tool may lead to a lack of understanding of the data

Overall, Compose AI's NLG software can be a useful tool for automating the process of creating written or spoken content from structured data. However, the quality of the generated content may vary depending on the data source, and it is essential to review the generated content before using it in a production environment. It is important to use the tool as an aid, not a replacement for the understanding of the data.

Conclusion

AI tools are becoming increasingly important in today's business and technology landscape. They are designed to automate repetitive tasks, improve workflow, and increase productivity. The top 10 AI tools included in this article are some of the most advanced and widely used in the market, and are suitable for various applications. Whether you're looking to improve your natural language processing, create high-resolution images, or optimize your website, there is an AI tool that can help. It's important to research and evaluate the different tools available to determine which one is the best fit for your specific needs. As AI technology continues to evolve, these tools will become even more powerful and versatile and will play an even greater role in shaping the future of business and technology.

#9561. Reconstructing Arabic PDFs to Word (.docx): Solving Ligatures, BiDi & Tables in Python

Converting PDF documents into clean, editable Microsoft Word (.docx) files has been a solved problem in English and Latin scripts for over a decade.

In the Arabic language, however, it has notoriously remained a nightmare.

If you have ever tried copying text or converting an Arabic PDF with mainstream tools, you have likely encountered this painful reality:

In this deep dive, we break down the exact engineering architecture we developed to solve Arabic PDF document reconstruction, which powers our production converter at hibdf.com and our commercial Python document engine.

Unlike Latin characters which maintain static visual representations regardless of position, Arabic is an inherently cursive script. Every character has up to four distinct glyph forms:

PDF format specifications (ISO 32000) store text as independent visual glyph coordinates on a two-dimensional canvas rather than semantic grammatical strings. When naive PDF parsers extract raw byte codes without a proper Unicode ToUnicode CMap table, they extract presentation-form glyph IDs rather than base Unicode code points.

Arabic is read right-to-left (RTL), but numbers, phone numbers, and embedded Latin terms (like brand names or code snippets) are read left-to-right (LTR).

When extracting text lines, if coordinates are sorted simply by increasing X coordinates ($X_0 \to X_1$), the words end up backwards. Sorting strictly by decreasing X coordinates breaks numbers like 2026 into 6202.

In standard Latin documents, columns read $C_1 \to C_2 \to C_3$ from left to right. In Arabic legal, financial, and academic documents, tables flow strictly from right to left: $$\text{Header}_0 \text{ (Rightmost)} \to \text{Header}_1 \to \text{Header}_2 \text{ (Leftmost)}$$

To achieve 100% fidelity without broken ligatures or inverted tables, we designed a sequential 4-stage pipeline:

The first step is handling presentation forms. When PDFs contain pre-rendered ligatures (such as لا U+FEFB or لله U+FDF2), we map them back to their canonical decomposition code points:

To guarantee that embedded numbers, currencies (e.g. $9.00 or 150 JOD), and English words remain left-to-right while Arabic sentences flow right-to-left:

The crucial step that 90% of open-source converters fail to implement is configuring Microsoft Word's underlying OpenXML schema for native Arabic RTL paragraphs and tables:

We deployed this exact architecture into two commercial production channels:

A fast, zero-install, cloud-optimized web application dedicated to converting Arabic PDFs into Word documents:

For developers and agencies looking to integrate automated document parsing, WhatsApp e-commerce, and client invoicing into their own stacks without monthly SaaS fees:

Handling Arabic digital typography is not about brute-force string manipulation; it requires respecting the mathematical and typographic rules of the language at both the Unicode abstraction layer and the OpenXML document format.

By combining layout bounding-box segmentation with contextual shaping and native OpenXML injection, we turned what used to be a broken output into an effortless, professional conversion workflow.

#9560. 2 Personality Traits Linked To A Stronger Immune System

Certain personality traits influence the body’s immune system response.

Certain personality traits influence the body’s immune system response.

People with more stable emotions have stronger immune systems, research finds.

People who are emotionally stable usually find it easier to control their urges and are mostly unselfconscious.

Emotional stability is linked to being better at dealing with stress and minor frustrations.

Neuroticism lies at the opposite end of the spectrum from emotional stability.

People who are neurotic typically experience more negative thinking and tend to have worse mental health.

The study included 84 people whose response to a vaccine for hepatitis B was tested.

The results showed that people who were more neurotic — meaning easily stressed, nervous and moody — tended to have weaker immune system responses.

Those who were more emotional stable had a stronger immune response.

Dr Anna L. Marsland,, the study’s first author, said:

“The present findings support a link between trait negative affect and an objective health measure — antibody response to vaccination — raising the possibility that individuals high in trait negative affect or neuroticism may have less protective immune responses.”

In a second part of the study, people were given a stressful task to test their immune function.

The results showed that stress tended to lower people’s immune system response — as previous studies have found.

Along with emotional stability, extraversion has also been linked to a stronger immune system, by a genetic analysis.

Extraverts are typically outgoing, talkative and energetic, meaning they tend to interact with more people.

They are, therefore, exposed to more infections.

A stronger immune response may help to protect extraverts against infectious diseases.

Introverts, meanwhile, tend to have a weaker immune response, as do cautious people.

The study included 121 people who were given personality questionnaires, along with genetic tests and general health screening.

The results showed that extraverts had the highest expression of pro-inflammatory genes.

The effect of these genes is to help fight off infections.

Introverts and cautious conscientious people tended to have a lower inflammatory response.

The study was published in the journal Health Psychology (Marsland et al., 2001).
