#9459. The Companies Allegedly Behind 15 Trader Joe's Items

Trader Joe's is full of unique and delicious products sold under the brand's private label, but having the store's name on the package doesn't mean that's who is making those products. Like other private label retailers like Aldi and Costco, Trader Joe's keeps the identity of its vendors under wraps to help keep costs lower for consumers. This probably means very little to the average Trader Joe's customer until beloved Trader Joe's products are discontinued and the search for a suitable replacement begins.

Importantly, just because a brand is confirmed or believed to be behind a Trader Joe's product doesn't mean that the Trader Joe's item is identical to the brand's usual offering. Small recipe or ingredient changes to adhere to Trader Joe's product standards and vendor requirements aren't uncommon.

Still, knowing the vendor can help you find a close match. While the legal agreements that keep Trader Joe's brands a secret usually make it nearly impossible to confirm the companies behind the store's products, several brands have been outed over the years. This is thanks to a combination of discerning customers, loose lipped employees, and a food safety policy that errs on the side of caution, resulting in an abundance of Trader Joe's recalls.

When it comes to foods like nuts, it's nearly impossible to tell one brand from another simply by looking at them, especially if the nuts in question don't have any special seasonings or flavors. That's certainly the case for pistachios roasted in their shells, which look virtually identical across brands, but a 2016 Salmonella-related recall helped unmask the major brand behind Trader Joe's pistachios as Wonderful Pistachios.

Three versions of Trader Joe's dry roasted, in shell pistachios were included in the recall: salted, unsalted, and 50% less salt. While the shelled version of Trader Joe's pistachios (unroasted, unsalted pistachio nutmeats) were not included in the recall and therefore can't definitively be linked to Wonderful, it is notable that the packaging for the shelled version is nearly identical to the dry roasted, in shell version, and Trader Joe's notes that both versions originate in California. Take that for what it's worth.

Salad kits and prepared salads are a convenient way to add extra veggies to your meal, and Trader Joe's has some delicious options. The brand behind those salads is one you've almost certainly heard. In August 2026, a large recall for fresh jalapeños contaminated with Salmonella had ripple effects across the food industry because of the number of brands that used the peppers in its products. Among those was Taylor Farms, which issued a recall on a number of different products, including Trader Joe's fiesta style salad with shrimp sold in Texas.

Around the same time, during a large scale outbreak of Cyclospora related illnesses also linked to Taylor Farms, an alleged Trader Joe's employee revealed on Reddit that the store sources most of its salad kits from Taylor Farms. At the time, the source of those illnesses had not yet been narrowed down to iceberg lettuce, and the seemingly well meaning employee posted the revelation as a public service announcement. The outbreak was declared over by the Centers for Disease Control on September 11, 2026.

Many Trader Joe's prepared foods and meals are perfect for a picnic, and you might be surprised how many of them are made by the same company. Bakkavor Foods USA has been behind many Trader Joe's products for at least a decade and was one of the largest producers of fresh and prepared foods in both the United States and the UK before being acquired by Greencore in 2025.

In 2016, Bakkavor issued a voluntary recall of both Trader Joe's Mediterranean Hummus and White Bean & Basil Hummus due to possible contamination with Listeria monocytogenes. But hummus isn't the only food that Bakkavor produces for Trader Joe's. Three years later in 2019, another voluntary recall was issued, again for possible listeria contamination, but this time in Trader Joe's Egg Salad and Old Fashioned Potato Salad. Then, in 2023, the company issued a recall for Trader Joe's Genova Pesto because it was incorrectly packaged and contained undeclared allergens in the form of milk and walnuts, both of which can cause serious allergic reactions.

After being acquired by Greencore, Bakkavor issued another recall in 2026 for Trader Joe's Focaccia Bread with Roasted Tomato & Parmesan. Metal fragments were discovered in the bread, which the company later said came from its roasted tomato supplier.

While the sugar content and some of the health claims made by Naked Juice have come under fire over the years, there's no denying that the brand makes delicious juice and smoothies. To hear some customers tell it, those same juices can be found at Trader Joe's.

Based on labels alone, those customers may be onto something. The ingredients in Trader Joe's Very Green 100% juice smoothie are a very close match to Naked's Green Machine and Trader Joe's Mango 100% juice smoothie is virtually a carbon copy of Naked's Mighty Mango Machine.

While that may be as close as we can get to confirmation today, Naked Juice and Trader Joe's go back more than two decades. In 2000, when possible Salmonella contamination resulted in a fresh juice recall in California, both Naked Juice and Trader Joe's juice were included as both were sourced from California Day-Fresh Foods at the time.

Naked Juice isn't the only brand behind the juice at Trader Joe's, at least as of 2024. Back then, a recall of under-processed organic carrot juice that carried a risk of causing botulism revealed that Trader Joe's organic carrot juice was made by Barsotti. It really wasn't that much of a surprise given that the Barsotti bottle was virtually identical to the Trader Joe's bottle, from the shape all the way down (or up) to the green cap.

Still, it was good for the carrot juice lovers to get confirmation, especially because Trader Joe's does not currently sell the organic carrot juice, and many customers miss it. Based on social media posts, it seemed to disappear from Trader Joe's shelves right around the time of the recall and never reappeared.

Trader Joe's does list an organic carrot turmeric juice blend on its website, but Barsotti does not sell a similar juice blend. Still, it's possible the carrot juice in the current juice blend originates with Barsotti and is a special recipe exclusive for Trader Joe's, but at this point, that's merely speculation.

While it is just one of many Trader Joe's myths that've been debunked that the grocery store is a spot for health food, the company does have pretty stringent standards for its products, and organic foods are easy to find. Combining both organic ingredients and a popular comfort food, the organic shells and white cheddar macaroni and cheese is long believed to be the same as Annie's organic Shells & White Cheddar macaroni and cheese.

The Trader Joe's version of the creamy comfort dish has ingredients that match Annie's almost exactly. If the ingredient similarities are not evidence enough, a packaging mistake in 2026 sealed the deal. Several customers posted photos online after allegedly opening their Trader Joe's Organic Shells and White Cheddar macaroni and cheese, only to find Annie's branded white cheddar powdered cheese packets inside. Whoops. That all but confirms it for sure.

Trader Joe's customers have expressed a lot of thoughts online about the store's meat and poultry selection. Some prefer it over what they find elsewhere, while others suggest it is expensive and subpar. But, like the other private label products at Trader Joe's, it may be the same meat and poultry you've bought elsewhere under a different name.

Whether Kayem still supplies the sausages is unclear, though the Trader Joe's website suggests the sausages are unchanged since they were introduced in 2004. Falling in love with a seasonal tea at Trader Joe's, only to have it discontinued is a terrible feeling. Many customers have found what they believe is a workaround. One of the most convincing arguments is a Reddit thread that focuses on Trader Joe's Candy Cane green tea. Not only are the ingredients identical to Celestial Seasonings Candy Cane Lane green tea, the boxes bear a striking resemblance with green clad polar bears on the front and the same box shape and design. Customers also suggest that Trader Joe's discontinued Red Refresh herbal tea is almost identical to Red Zinger by Celestial Seasonings in taste, description, and packaging.

One commenter alleges that they personally saw Trader Joe's mango tea boxes when they went on the Celestial Seasonings factory tour and recounts being told by the tour guide that Celestial Seasonings makes other teas for the retailer. What we know for sure is that Celestial Seasonings publicly partnered with Trader Joe's for two exclusive tea blends in 2013 (Harvest Blend and Chai). While the company's website previously noted this as a milestone event on its history page (via Internet Archive), the information has since been removed.

Comparing Trader Joe's thin and crunchy pretzel slims with Snack Factory's original pretzel crisps, there are certainly some compelling similarities among the ingredients. Trader Joe's pretzel slims contain unbleached enriched flour, inverted sugar syrup, salt, malted barley, sodium bicarbonate (baking soda), and sodium hydroxide. Snack Factory's pretzel crisps contain enriched flour, cane sugar, salt, tapioca malt syrup, canola oil, and [baking] soda. The two varieties also share a 1-ounce serving size with matching calorie content. Thankfully, Snack Factory's dark chocolate variety is easier to find than Trader Joe's.

There's nothing like a bowl of warm soup in the fall and winter months, and few soups are as resoundingly praised as Trader Joe's organic tomato and roasted red pepper soup. Customers rave about eating the soup with grilled cheese sandwiches, macaroni and cheese balls, or even with a bit of rice mixed in to bulk it up as a standalone meal. If that has you craving a bowl for yourself but your Trader Joe's doesn't have any in stock, just pick up a carton of Pacific Food's roasted red pepper and tomato soup. A 2017 recall due to under-processing revealed they are both made by Pacific.

Although other varieties of Trader Joe's soups have not been recalled, and we therefore do not have a confirmation as to their manufacturer, the same style box that is used for the organic tomato and roasted red pepper soup (and Pacific soups) is also used for the store's organic chicken and vegetable broths, including regular and low sodium.

For folks with peanut allergies, Trader Joe's Dark Chocolate Almond Butter Cups can be a great alternative to the more common peanut butter cups. Unfortunately, a 2021 recall revealed that some of the almond butter cups might have inadvertently contained peanut protein. While the package label indicated traces of peanuts were possible, allergic reactions prompted the recall anyway. The recall also revealed the candy was produced by Bazzini.

Even if you don't know the name, you likely know the products. Bazzini started out in 1886, making it the oldest nut and confection company in the United States, and also the brand of peanuts sold at Yankee Stadium. Its chocolate confections are sold under the name Barton's and include not only dark chocolate almond butter cups, but also milk chocolate peanut butter cups and dark chocolate peanut butter cups. Both peanut butter cup varieties are also available at Trader Joe's and may also be produced by Bazzini.

Trader Joe's selection of snack foods is arguably only matched by its selection of frozen foods and meals, especially when it comes to international cuisine. It might not be too surprising to learn that the manufacturer behind at least some of these international frozen foods is Ajinomoto Foods, which purports to be the brand leader in the sector.

While we can't definitively say all the different products Ajinomoto provides to Trader Joe's, a large recall in early 2026 included Trader Joe's chicken fried rice. The recall was initially issued due to the possibility of glass fragments in several products across many different labels. Trader Joe's expanded on Ajinomoto's initial recall and included its vegetable fried rice, Japanese fried rice, and chicken Shu Mai to be on the safe side, confirming that all are Ajinomoto products. All of those are pretty popular TJ's products, too.

For those of us who love yogurt, Trader Joe's has plenty to choose from, and it's one of the few products whose origin is somewhat easy to pinpoint, even without a specific recall. In 2017, a writer for Fortune revealed that Stonyfield supplies Trader Joe's with a good deal of its yogurt, especially on the East Coast. Around the same time, a Trader Joe's employee confirmed Stonyfield was one of the store's partners during a Reddit Ask Me Anything session.

Even though Stonyfield had one of the worst yogurt recalls in history, that was also all the way back in 2017 and applied only to plant-based yogurt, none of which was recalled from Trader Joe's. But tracking the manufacturer of Trader Joe's yogurt is a lot easier than some other products due to the ease with which consumers can track dairy manufacturing in the United States using the website Where Is My Milk From.

Dairy plant codes used by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) are stamped on all containers and can be traced to specific manufacturers. For example, Trader Joe's yogurt with dairy codes that begin with 33-14 originate at the Stonyfield plant in Londonderry, New Hampshire.

The holiday season is one of the best times of the year for foodies because all sorts of seasonal gourmet condiments and snacks start to hit the shelves at Trader Joe's. Among these are jams, jellies, spreads, and bar mixes, all of which can be perfect additions to holiday celebrations.

The problem is that once they're gone, they're gone. That is, unless you are a discerning customer who is able to figure out that Trader Joe's Step Up to the Snack Bar mix, discontinued garlic and onion jam, and pepper jelly are all dead ringers for the same products at Stonewall Kitchen. In particular, Trader Joe's and Stonewall Kitchen's bar mixes both contain honey roasted peanuts, honey mustard pretzels, cheddar crackers, sesame sticks, and chili lemon sticks.

Unfortunately, neither the garlic and onion jam nor the pepper jelly are currently available at Trader Joe's, but they've been known to make a comeback seasonally. If you simply can't wait, Stonewall Kitchen sells them year-round.

#9456. Aggressive Policing as a Public Health Issue

The medical field has paid increased attention to the negative health impacts of systemic racism, discrimination, poverty, and other societal forces that are known to cause poorer health. This includes awareness of the need to assess and address racial and other health disparities and focus on principles of diversity, equity, and inclusion. We have moved beyond the framing of these issues as moral imperatives to understanding how they are related to individual and public health.

Discussion of the health harms of aggressive policing has also increased over the last 2 years, spurred by the frequent and well-publicized deaths of Black, Indigenous, and people of color (BIPOC). What has been viewed as a political issue is now understood as a public health/health inequity concern. Two articles that have helped change the way the medical community views these issues were published in 2021:

Both of these pieces help illustrate the ongoing shift in how police violence and aggressive policing have specific and disproportionate impacts on communities of color.

The first article makes several key points in its assertion that policing concerns should be viewed as health issues. It begins with this statement:

“Marginalized communities have a long history of naming the systemic racism and harms of police violence to health and well-being and recognizing their roots in the oppression of Black and Indigenous communities.”

The article cites data indicating that BIPOC are far more likely to be killed by police than White Americans, noting that death at the hands of a police officer is the sixth leading cause of death for young Black men. Similarly, Black and Indigenous women are more likely to be killed by a police officer than their White counterparts.

The second article also looks at specific data related to the disparate impact of what is describes as the “overexposure” to aggressive policing strategies among Black communities, serving to increase already existing health disparities in such communities. The article authors noted:

“Indeed, aggressive policing strategies employed by law enforcement agencies across the country have been hypothesized to degrade health and well-being, even among people who themselves have not experienced contact with police. Perhaps even more important, aggressive policing is thought to contribute to significant population health inequities, as these practices are concentrated on — and thus exacerbate — the health challenges faced by racialized populations.”

The authors of the article cited data from an organization called Campaign Zero.3 This group’s website includes data that also helps demonstrated the negative impact of aggressive policing, or what they describe as “broken windows” policing. This form of policing has led to the overpolicing of communities of color with resulting excessive force, leading to unnecessary deaths.

“Meanwhile, the vast majority of arrests are for low-level, nonviolent activities in encounters that often escalate to deadly force. For example, in 2014, police killed at least 287 people who were involved in minor offenses and harmless activities like sleeping in parks, possessing drugs, looking “suspicious” or having a mental health crisis. These activities are often symptoms of underlying issues of drug addiction, homelessness, and mental illness, which should be treated by health care professionals and social workers rather than the police.”

These 3 examples of the evolving understanding of how to view police aggressiveness highlight the need for future research and data collection. They also highlight the need for PAs, nurse practitioners, and other medical providers to assess the health impact of high-impact policing on their patients and to advocate for changes to a policing system that results in furthering existing health disparities.

1. Fleming PJ, Lopez WD, Spolum M, Anderson RE, Reyes AG, Schulz AJ. Policing is a public health issue: the important role of health educators. Health Educ Behav. 2021:10901981211001010. doi:10.1177/10901981211001010

2. Esposito M, Larimore S, Lee H. Aggressive policing, health, and health equity. Health Policy Brief. Health Affairs. April 30, 2021. doi:10.1377/hpb20210412.997570.

3. Campaign Zero. https://www.joincampaignzero.org/solutions#solutionsoverview

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9455. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

Many desserts can be intimidatingly complex, requiring both difficult technique and extensive ingredients. That need not always be the case, though. For a delicious batch of brigadeiros – an iconic Brazilian dessert – preparation starts with a simple can of sweetened condensed milk. The sweet is essentially like a chewy chocolate truffle, constructed using a trio of cocoa powder, butter, and the cornerstone condensed milk. The assembly is as straightforward as the ingredients. All components are simmered together over low heat for around twenty minutes to thicken, then cooled and formed into bite-sized balls.

Although easy to make, the dessert is delicious and playful. The condensed milk lends each bite a signature caramel-like sweetness, balanced out by the cocoa bitterness. The dessert is made to a soft consistency, but often coated with fun garnishes like chocolate sprinkles, nuts, or coconut flakes, yielding an intriguing textural contrast. Arranged on a plate, it's a surprising way to use condensed milk with an impressive result.

With Brigidiaro's three-ingredient composition, every element plays a role in the final flavor. Not all cans of sweetened condensed milk are alike. Some taste sweeter, others more caramel-forward, all while varying in texture, too. As the sole source of sugar in the dessert, the type you choose defines its sweetness. For example, regular granulated sugar is a blank canvas, ready to take on the cocoa flavor while brown sugars have a little note of molasses. Want to fine-tune the brigidiaro even further? Consider making your own sweetened condensed milk at home using solely milk and sugar.

In parallel, the employed cocoa powder also makes a noticeable difference. The foodstuff's treatment influences the taste –  a Dutch process will feature less acidity, for example. And for even more control over the Brigidairo's chocolate taste, consider shaving a chocolate bar, one of the easiest substitutes for cocoa powder. With such an inclusion, you can vary the cocoa composition. An 85% cocoa powder will lend the brigidairo more complex dark and earthy notes, while a milder 50% makes for an extra sweet and creamy experience.

Butter serves as a fat that brings the components together. Go for a classic unsalted stick; there's no need for an extra flavorful cultured butter or a higher-fat European-style. And once the fat has melted, you could optionally stir in flavorings like lemon juice and zest (use white chocolate or skip it altogether for this) or spices such as nutmeg and cinnamon to add subtle warmth throughout your dessert. All held together with a three-ingredient foundation, brigadeiros welcome a multitude of subtle twists.

#9453. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

Cover photo by Mark Weinberg; food styling by Liz Neily.

#9452. 7 types of anxiety disorders (and how to deal with each one)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Your heart starts racing the moment you walk into a crowded room. Even when nothing’s wrong, worry looms in the back of your mind. The thought of a specific fear, like snakes or needles, makes you feel sick. If any of that sounds familiar, anxiety might be part of the picture.

Anxiety doesn't look the same for everyone, which is sometimes why it can be so hard to name. The term "anxiety" covers several disorders, each with its own signs and triggers — though they often overlap, both in how they show up and in what helps.

Anxiety disorders affect roughly 1 in 5 U.S. adults every year. The good news is, they’re typically quite treatable. Let’s break down the seven main types of anxiety listed in the DSM-5 (the manual used for clinical diagnosis), and how to find some relief.

The seven anxiety disorders below share a general thread: they’re rooted in fear or worry that sticks around and gets in the way of daily life. They’re also the most common types, though a few related conditions are worth knowing too (covered further down).

GAD is a persistent, hard-to-control worry that spans multiple areas of your life and shows up more days than not for at least six months. Everyday stress usually has a clear cause and fades once the situation resolves. By contrast, generalized anxiety moves from topic to topic and rarely lets up, because your mind treats any uncertainty as a threat.

This disorder often comes with physical and mental symptoms such as restlessness, muscle tension, fatigue, trouble concentrating, irritability, and disrupted sleep.

What helps: Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is widely used for GAD. It helps you spot and shift the thought patterns that fuel your worries. A regular mindfulness practice can also ease tension by training your attention to stay in the present instead of running through what-ifs.

💙 Start with Calm’s Tools for Stress and Anxiety series.

For a more detailed overview, check out our GAD guide.

A panic attack is a sudden rush of intense fear that brings on physical symptoms—racing heart, tight chest, dizziness—and usually peaks within minutes. A single panic attack doesn't mean you have panic disorder — plenty of people experience one and never have another.

Panic disorder is defined by what comes after the attack, such as ongoing dread about when the next one might hit and routine changes made to avoid triggering one.

This fear response tends to feed itself in a cycle. A normal body signal, like a fast heartbeat, gets misread as danger. That triggers more fear, which leads to more physical symptoms.

What helps: CBT can help you learn to read these body signals as harmless rather than dangerous. It’s often paired with interoceptive exposure, where you deliberately bring on mild versions of those same sensations until they stop feeling threatening. During this process, slow breathing can signal safety to your nervous system.

Discover 5 mindfulness tools to calm you down during a panic attack.

Social anxiety disorder is a strong fear that you’ll be negatively perceived in social or performance situations, often severe enough that dread sets in days before the event itself.

It's much more than being shy. At its core is a belief that you'll do something embarrassing and be judged for it. That belief may lead you to avoid those situations altogether, which can bring short-term relief but reinforces the fear over time.

What helps: Exposure-based CBT has the strongest evidence. It gradually builds your comfort in the situations you've been avoiding by facing them in small, manageable steps. Self-compassion can also make a real difference. Since social anxiety tends to run on harsh self-judgment, practicing kindness toward yourself can help quiet that inner critic.

Not sure if you have social anxiety? Here are signs to look out for.

A specific phobia is a fear of one particular thing—like heights, flying, needles, dogs, or tight spaces—out of proportion to the actual danger. A fear becomes a phobia when it impacts your behavior, whether that’s rerouting a drive to avoid a bridge or skipping a checkup because of needles. Even thinking about the trigger can set off anxiety, so avoiding it becomes your default.

Phobias often start with a scary experience or a fear picked up early in life. Avoidance keeps the fear alive, since your brain never learns that the trigger is safe.

What helps: Exposure therapy is the leading treatment, shown to outperform placebo and other therapies. Pair each step with grounding and breathing techniques to make the process feel more manageable.

Explore the most common phobias and how to deal with them.

Agoraphobia is a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help if panic or embarrassing symptoms hit. This can include public transit, open spaces, crowds, lines, or long stretches away from home alone. Many people with agoraphobia avoid those places altogether.

The DSM-5 classifies it as its own diagnosis. Left untreated, this avoidance can shrink your world, sometimes making it hard to leave the house at all.

What helps: CBT with step-by-step exposure is the first-line treatment, and it helps you return to avoided places gradually. Since agoraphobia and panic often overlap, treatment usually addresses both. To build confidence, try calming techniques at home first, then in triggering places.

Learn 8 evidence-backed ways to manage agoraphobia.

Separation anxiety disorder is an excessive fear about being away from people you're close to. Once seen as a childhood condition, it’s now known to affect adults too. It can show up as real distress when a partner travels or constant worry that something bad will happen to a loved one.

Underneath it is a fear of loss: of the person or of your own ability to cope without them. You may find yourself seeking reassurance or checking in repeatedly, but these responses tend to feed the anxiety rather than calm it.

What helps: CBT can help you reduce your need for reassurance and build comfort with time apart. Mindfulness encourages you to pause when an anxious thought arises and let the worry pass. For severe cases, a doctor may suggest therapy alongside medication.

💙 Practice riding out anxious thoughts with Calm’s Letting Go of Anxiety course.

Selective mutism is an inability to speak in certain social settings where talking is expected, like school or work. It's rare, affecting under 2% of people, and it usually shows up in childhood, though it can last into later years.

This isn't stubbornness or a speech problem — it's fear. You may want to speak, but hold back because of it in those environments.

What helps: Behavioral therapy that slowly builds up speaking in those settings, often involving family or school staff, is the main approach. Early intervention tends to lead to better outcomes, so it’s worth seeking professional guidance as soon as symptoms appear.

While the disorders above are what most people mean by "anxiety," a few related conditions are helpful to understand for the full picture.

Two more fall under the DSM-5's anxiety chapter:

Substance or medication-induced anxiety disorder: This anxiety is caused directly by a substance, whether that’s too much caffeine, a prescription drug, or withdrawal from alcohol. It can be overlooked, which is why a doctor will often ask what you're taking before making a diagnosis.

Anxiety disorder due to another medical condition: A physical illness—such as an overactive thyroid or a heart or lung problem—can cause anxiety. A checkup can rule out this possibility early on, and treating the underlying illness often eases the anxiety too.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) get grouped with anxiety disorders a lot, as they also involve overwhelming fear and distress. But the DSM-5 classifies them separately: OCD centers on unwanted thoughts and behaviors, while PTSD comes after a traumatic event.

If either sounds closer to what you're dealing with, our OCD guide or our complex PTSD guide is a good place to start.

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and panic disorder differ mainly in how the worry builds and shows up. GAD involves a slow-burning worry about many areas of life that rarely fades. Panic disorder centers on sudden, intense attacks and the fear of having another one. It’s possible to have both, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) works well for either.

Curious about CBT for anxiety? Here are 5 techniques to try.

The difference between having social anxiety and being introverted comes down to preference versus fear. Introversion is a preference about how you recharge — social time drains your energy, but it doesn't fill you with dread. Social anxiety, meanwhile, brings a fear of judgment or embarrassment, often strong enough to make you skip things you'd enjoy.

It’s not unusual to have more than one anxiety disorder at the same time, and they can show up alongside other conditions including depression. A doctor can help you sort out which ones you’re dealing with, and treatments like CBT can target several disorders at once.

A specific phobia and agoraphobia differ in what the fear is tied to. A specific phobia is about one clear trigger, such as spiders or flying. Agoraphobia is broader: it's a fear of being somewhere you couldn't easily escape or get help, like a crowd or public transit.

The most common types of anxiety in adults are specific phobias, social anxiety disorder, and generalized anxiety disorder. Altogether, anxiety disorders affect close to 1 in 5 U.S. adults each year and are the most prevalent type of mental health condition.

Anxiety disorders can ease on their own for some people, but many stick around or return without treatment. Fortunately, treatment can meaningfully improve your quality of life. Most people find that therapy, medication, or a combination makes a noticeable difference.

The most well-supported therapy for anxiety disorders is cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), often paired with gradual exposure work. Medication is another option with strong evidence, either used alone or alongside therapy. The right fit depends on your specific disorder and its severity, so it's important to consult a professional.

There are several natural ways to manage anxiety, though they aren’t a replacement for clinical treatment. Regular exercise, quality sleep, and cutting back on caffeine and alcohol can all help alleviate how anxious you feel day to day. Mindfulness practices (like breathing exercises or grounding techniques) are especially well-supported, since they teach you to notice anxious thoughts or sensations without getting swept up in them.

Mental health is hard. Getting support doesn't have to be. The Calm app puts the tools to feel better in your back pocket, with personalized content to manage stress and anxiety, get better sleep, and feel more present in your life.

#9450. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9446. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

Cover photo by Patrick Marinello; food styling by Yekaterina Boytsova.

Justine Lee is a food writer, recipe developer, and culinary consultant based in New York City. In her free time, she is actively on a hunt for a good almond croissant.

#9444. COVID-19 and Moral Injury: a Mental Health Pandemic for Frontline Health Care Workers

More than 2 years ago, the alarm and first warnings of a global pandemic sounded. Now with over 830,000 deaths caused by COVID-19 in the US, there looms on the horizon a second underlying curve with equally serious long-term consequences: a mental health pandemic.

The mental health fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic demands recognition, intervention, and mitigation strategies. Among the many at-risk populations are frontline health care workers who have been at the epicenter of the global pandemic, working long shifts with at times a tenuous safety net and limited support, and caring for COVID-19 patients with limited resources, mixed messaging, and uncertainty with regards to an end to the crisis. The psychological effects in some health care providers are akin to the moral trauma or moral injury that is recognized in combat veterans with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

Mental health professionals and other health care providers caring for frontline health care workers who present with insomnia, depression, anxiety, panic attacks, PTSD, and suicidal thoughts should recognize and validate their experiences and moral injury. Intervention strategies including health promotion, resilience training, and ongoing multilevel support will play an important role in flattening the moral injury curve.

As a rule, the frontline health care workforce is considered capable, competent, resilient, professional, and persevering in the face of adversity. However, COVID-19 presented as an unprecedented crisis unlike any other unforeseen disaster, eliciting fear, uncertainty, and anxiety, coupled with grief and loss, both personally and professionally.1 As noted by Warren D. Taylor, MD, MHSc, and Jennifer Urbano Blackford, PhD1:

The pandemic created anxiety and fear in health care providers, from physicians and nurses to allied health professionals and first-line responders. We fear for the safety of our families and patients. We grieve for those who have died. We feel guilt for not being able to save all our patients, for getting sick ourselves, and for abandoning our families. Many adopted the phrase, “we will get through this together but none of us will survive unscathed.”

At the outset, the shortage of equipment and resources, changing practice guidelines, and unpredictability of the workload rendered health care workers with a sense of powerlessness and loss of control of the conditions under which they were able to deliver care. The emotional distress and social isolation from family and friends exacted an immeasurable toll on the physical health and emotional well-being of the workforce, setting the stage for the inevitable moral injury.2

Moral injury is a term that has been applied to veterans of combat. Moral injury or moral distress as experienced by frontline health care providers occurs when health care providers are forced to make decisions that transgress their professional commitment to patient comfort and care, and forcibly shift their moral compass. They are not able to meet the physical, emotional, and end-of-life needs of patients.3

Watson et al noted that moral injury in health care workers “can occur when someone engages in, fails to prevent, or witnesses acts that conflict with their values or beliefs.”4 Moral injuries may result from the following, according to Watson et al4:

The consequences of such experiences may include feelings of rage, guilt, shame, and anger and moral injury is the “lasting psychological, spiritual, behavioral or social impact that may result from these experiences.”4 The number of acutely ill COVID-19 patients and high death rate coupled with lack of resources and at times rationing of limited resources such as personal protective equipment (PPE) and ventilators added to the dilemma that frontline health care workers faced.

In a study of 448 Jordanian nurses during the COVID-19 pandemic, the majority of nurses (64%) reported experiencing acute stress disorder (ASD) and 41% reported significant psychological distress, with a predilection for younger nurses compared to older nurses.5 However, coping self-efficacy was a protective factor with the potential to mitigate the severity of psychological distress.5 An online survey of nonhealth care providers (N=976) found that individuals with previous trauma were at highest risk for increased symptoms of anxiety, depression, and PTSD related to COVID-19 compared with individuals with no previous history of trauma.6

The long-term mental health consequences of moral injury for frontline health care workers have important implications for workforce survivability and durability; however, research on this topic is lacking. In one of the few published studies on moral injury among health care providers, investigators looked at the thematic content of experiences reported by nurses following incidents meeting the contextual definition of moral injury (ie, events with unintended consequences, potentially causing patient harm or putting patients at risk for serious injury). The investigators found nurses reported experiencing “guilt, shame, spiritual–existential crisis, and loss of trust.”7

COVID-19 has presented difficult and untenable working conditions beyond the scope of the challenges frontline health care workers are prepared for professionally. Frontline health care workers have experienced conflict and distress over prioritizing patient care vs their own safety, protecting family members from infection, and the reality that the supplies, medications, and equipment needed to save a life were not always available or were being rationed. Because of high infectivity, morbidity, and mortality associated with the spread of the virus, frontline health care workers were often in the position to be the only person at the bedside at the end of life with patients who were separated from their families. This is not how families should experience the loss of a loved one.4

There is a body of research regarding the long-term effects of moral injury among combat soldiers.3 It is reasonable to expect that feelings of guilt, shame, anger, and self-recrimination stemming from moral injury in these soldiers may be similar to feelings experienced by frontline health care workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and that their experiences increase the risk for acute stress reactions with long-term consequences including increased incidence of depression, anxiety, substance abuse, PTSD, and suicide.4,8 Behavior changes including intrusive memories, avoidance of situations that are reminders of prior events, self-isolation, and potential triggers of traumatic memories are common in individuals suffering from acute stress disorder or PTSD. Additional responses to stress, trauma, and moral injury include disturbed sleep, emotional changes such as numbing, desensitization, depersonalization, and a decreased capacity for empathy and compassion. For some individuals, the consequences of moral injury may be an opportunity for reflection and reprioritization of values and an existential inner process of reflecting on what is important in life.4

Given the consequences of moral injury, it is important for mental health professionals and health care providers treating frontline health care providers to recognize and identify those experiences that have the potential for promoting resilience.9

An analysis of data from 2,579 frontline health care workers in New York City early on in the pandemic showed that key factors predictive of psychological resilience were positive emotions, self-efficacy, purpose in life, strong social support, and not engaging in maladaptive coping strategies (eg, substance abuse).9 Psychological resilience was described by the authors as, “the capacity to adapt and thrive while facing adversity or challenging circumstances,” leading to the question of how can institutions promote psychological resilience in frontline health care workers?9

Initiativespromoting psychological resilience are critical.10,11 Interventions identifying those at high risk for moral injury and in need of support in the form of psychological first-aid and psychotherapy have the potential of improving resilience. Kameno et al administered the short-form of the Kessler Psychological Distress Scale with 4 additional questions, 2 regarding sleep, 1 on appetite changes, and 1 on alcohol misuse, in health care workers during the pandemic.12 The researchers found that women and nurses had higher rates of affective symptoms compared to men and other medical staff, respectively. The researchers noted that early identification and psychotherapy may improve psychological resilience and reduce psychological distress in nurses at high risk for maladaptive coping.12

The need for institutional support, leadership support, education, and training is equally important. Leadership and management are challenged to identify those practices that address the needs of their respective health care workers.10 Survey findings on the expectations and needs of health care workers (physicians, nurses, advanced practice clinicians, residents, and fellows; N=69) during the first week of the pandemic at a single hospital identified the following 5 requests of their organization: hear me, protect me, prepare me, support me, and care for me.13 Management and leadership have the opportunity to promote resilience and show visible support for the health care workforce with unique initiatives to help reduce and mitigate the long-term consequences of moral injury and acute stress response.

Similar to triage protocols and models to meet emergent health care systems demands from unexpected disasters, there is a need for a multilayered mental health care response for frontline workers. Self-care and wellness initiatives have the potential to reduce the long-term consequences of moral injury. Ongoing support, skills training, psychoeducation, and wellness education regarding strategies to address and process the experiences of frontline health care workers are critical for healing the wounds of moral injury. Empathic sensitivity on the part of mental health providers and primary care providers is essential. Listening to “the story” and having the opportunity to process and reflect on the self-talk related to the experience of moral injury can lay the groundwork for healing.

Self-care needs should include the opportunity to seek out and have available a support system of peers and colleagues. All too often the experience of shame, guilt, and self-condemnation are obstacles to seeking self-help and lead to self-isolation. If allowed to process and reflect on those experiences, health care workers may be provided an opportunity for experiential growth and a redefinition of priorities personally and professionally.

Leaders in health care have the opportunity to create and foster a culture of open, nonjudgmental communication. In the face of unpredictable events such as the COVID-19 pandemic, natural disasters, and social and political unrest that impact health care delivery, strategies are available to promote mental health recovery and return to stability and wellness among frontline health care workers.

Catherine R. Judd, MS, PA-C, CAQ-Psy, DFAAPA, is an assistant clinical professor in the Department of Physician Assistant Studies at the School of Health Professions, The University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center, Dallas, Texas.

1. Taylor WD, Blackford JU. Mental health treatment for front-line clinicians during and after the coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic: a plea to the medical community. Ann Intern Med. 2020;173(7):574-575. doi:10.7326/M20-2440

2. Hossain F, Clatty A. Self-care strategies in response to nurses’ moral injury during COVID-19 pandemic. Nurs Ethics. 2021;28(1):23-32. doi:10.1177/0969733020961825

3. Borges LM, Barnes SM, Farnsworth JK, Bahraini NH, Brenner LA. A commentary on moral injury among health care providers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychol Trauma. 2020;12(S1):S138-S140. doi:10.1037/tra0000698

4. Watson P, Norman SB, Maguen S, Hamblen J. Moral injury in health care workers. Accessed January 4, 2021. https://www.ptsd.va.gov/professional/treat/cooccurring/moral_injury_hcw.asp

5. Shahrour G, Dardas LA. Acute stress disorder, coping self-efficacy and subsequent psychological distress among nurses amid COVID-19. J Nurs Manag. 2020;28(7):1686-1695. doi:10.1111/jonm.13124

6. Lahav Y. Psychological distress related to COVID-19 — The contribution of continuous traumatic stress. J Affect Disord. 2020;277:129-137. doi:10.1016/j.jad.2020.07.141

7. Stovall M, Hansen L, van Ryn M. A critical review: moral injury in nurses in the aftermath of a patient safety incident. J Nurs Scholarsh. 2020;52(3):320-328. doi:10.1111/jnu.12551

8. Pappa S, Ntella V, Giannakas T, Giannakoulis VG, Papoutsi E, Katsaounou P. Prevalence of depression, anxiety, and insomnia among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Brain Behav Immun. 2020;88:901-907. doi:10.1016/j.bbi.2020.05.026

9. Pietrzak RH, Feingold JH, Feder A, Charney DS, Peccoralo L, Southwick SM, Ripp J. Psychological resilience in frontline health care workers during the acute phase of the COVID-19 pandemic in New York City. J Clin Psychiatry. 2020;82(1):20l13749. doi:10.4088/JCP.20l13749

10. Krystal JH, Alvarado J, Ball SA, et al. Mobilizing an institutional supportive response for healthcare workers and other staff in the context of COVID-19: the Yale experience. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:12-18. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.11.005

11. Park ER, Sylvia LG, Streck JM, et al. Launching a resiliency group program to assist frontline clinicians in meeting the challenges of the COVID-19 pandemic: results of a hospital-based systems trial. Gen Hosp Psychiatry. 2021;68:111-112. doi:10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2020.10.005

12. Kameno Y, Hanada A, Asai D, et al. Individual psychotherapy using psychological first aid for frontline nurses at high risk of psychological distress during the COVID-19 pandemic. Psychiatry Clin Neurosci. 2021;75(1):25-27. doi:10.1111/pcn.13170.

13. Shanafelt T, Ripp J, Trockel M. Understanding and addressing sources of anxiety among health care professionals during the COVID-19 pandemic. JAMA. 2020;323(21):2133-2134. doi:10.1001/jama.2020.5893

#9432. How to define cheating in a relationship (and what to do about it)

Clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA

Late-night texts lighting up their phone. A “friend from work” who comes up a little too often when they talk about their day. Or maybe it’s the other way around, and it’s a name you've conveniently left out of your story. Either way, it leads to a quiet, nagging sense that something's off.

Some cheating is obvious. But the old idea that it only counts if it's physical doesn't hold up to how people experience betrayal today. Emotional connections can form through a screen, and it isn't always a single, clear-cut act.

Here’s the big picture on what cheating really means, and what to do if you’re facing it in your own relationship.

Cheating means acting in a way that violates the boundaries and trust that a couple has built together.

The issue is that the boundaries aren’t always clear. Many couples never discuss what's off limits, whether that’s a text to an ex, a close emotional friendship, or a flirtatious dinner. You and your partner may share the same values, and assume you’re aligned on the specifics. Then a moment reveals you’re not.

Where people draw the line on cheating usually traces back to a few underlying factors.

Attachment style: People prone to relationship anxiety may read more behaviors as threatening. People who lean more avoidant may downplay concerning behavior as trivial, including their own.

Cultural and religious background: Some cultures and religions view certain dating norms, like close friendships outside the relationship, as completely normal, while others see them as concerning.

Relationship structure: Couples set their own rules for the relationship, whether that’s monogamy, non-monogamy, or somewhere in between. Those rules define what counts as betrayal.

Related read: How to find your attachment style and deepen your relationships

Infidelity takes many forms, and even within each form, it can look drastically different depending on the situation. Here’s how it tends to show up.

This is the one most people picture first: romantic or sexual contact with someone outside the relationship, without your partner knowing or agreeing to it. That last part is key.

Couples in open relationships can have very different lines. As long as both partners are on the same page, physical intimacy with others can be a normal part of the relationship.

Emotional cheating means forming a close bond with someone outside your relationship that pulls closeness or energy away from your partner.

The line between a close friendship and an emotional affair can feel blurry, but research points to three signs:

Details get shared that don't get shared with your partner.

An unspoken attraction exists, even if neither person names it.

Emotional cheating can be dismissed because nothing physical happened, but many people find it just as painful as physical infidelity, sometimes more so. It tends to build slowly, until the loyalty has quietly shifted.

Virtual cheating is physical or emotional cheating through a screen. This can look like sexting, intimate messaging, or building a close connection online. Some therapists also include excessive pornography use when it's hidden and gets in the way of intimacy with a partner, though opinions vary.

This type of cheating is more accessible than most other forms of infidelity, and is often harder to catch. A message is one tap away, at any hour, with virtually anyone.

Micro-cheating involves smaller, ambiguous behaviors that fall short of the categories above, but can still chip away at trust. Some common examples include:

Keeping a dating profile active "just in case"

Finding constant reasons to message one specific person

Spending time with someone without mentioning it to your partner

Flirting with someone in a way you wouldn't if your partner were present

It comes down to whether it's a repeated pattern your partner wouldn't be okay with.

Financial infidelity means hiding money, concealing debt, keeping secret accounts, or making big financial decisions without telling your partner. It's a serious trust issue, especially in long-term relationships where finances are shared.

This is more common than most people expect and can do just as much damage as other forms of infidelity.

If you’re suspicious of your partner, sitting with that uncertainty can feel unbearable. But before you act on a hunch, try slowing down and approaching the situation with as much calm as you can.

Start by noticing what’s actually happening—and what’s actually changed—versus what you suspect. Has your partner’s communication, availability, or emotional presence shifted in a specific way? Or is this more of a gut sense that something's off?

Both are valid, but knowing which one you’re dealing with can help you decide how to proceed.

💙 Explore Sensations vs. Emotions with Jay Shetty on Calm.

Your unease may not be about your suspicions. It might be disconnection, feeling unappreciated, or a sense that something’s changed between you. Getting clear on what’s bugging you before you bring it up can make the conversation more productive.

💙 Dig deeper with Investigating Anxiety from the Emotions Series on Calm.

You may think that checking their phone, socials, or location data will settle your suspicion about the situation. But it tends to worsen your anxiety.

If you find something, you’re left dealing with what you found and the fact that you went looking. If you don’t, the relief rarely lasts, because whatever made you suspicious in the first place is still unresolved.

A few minutes of focused breathing before a hard conversation can settle your body and quiet your mind. That short reset can help you feel steadier and lead to a clearer conversation for both of you.

💙 Take a Pause to Breathe on the Calm app.

Before you bring something up, think about what you’re hoping for. Do you want clarity? Reassurance? That goal can keep you focused, even if the conversation gets derailed.

Approaching the discussion with an open mind, rather than jumping to accusations, often invites a more honest exchange.

Instead of starting with “I think you’re cheating on me,” try something along the lines of “I’ve been feeling disconnected and I’d like to talk about it.”

Whether you're dealing with confirmed infidelity or unresolved suspicion, you don't have to process it alone. Support from a therapist, individually or as a couple, can offer a structured space to work through it.

Sometimes suspicion itself, even without proof of cheating, may be a sign that the relationship needs attention.

Cheating is a violation of the spoken or unspoken agreements you and your partner have made about exclusivity. It can show up physically, emotionally, or virtually, and what counts can look different from couple to couple. Secrecy and broken trust are usually the common thread.

Read more: Here's how to work through the most common relationship issues

The main types of cheating are physical, emotional, and virtual, though subtler patterns such as financial secrecy or "micro-cheating" can apply too.

Physical cheating involves intimate contact outside the relationship. Emotional cheating involves a close bond kept hidden from your partner. Virtual cheating involves a romantic connection through a screen.

Emotional cheating can feel just as harmful as physical cheating, and for some people, more so. It often builds slowly, through shared thoughts and private moments your partner doesn't know about.

Physical cheating usually involves specific, identifiable moments, while emotional cheating often unfolds gradually, as loyalty fades over time.

Cheating almost always involves some kind of concealment. Being vague, withholding details, or keeping a connection secret are all forms of it. Sometimes it's the hiding, more than the act itself, that turns it into a betrayal.

Couples can define cheating differently, based on their values, culture, and the specific agreements they've made. Partners in open relationships, for example, may knowingly allow behaviors that other couples wouldn't. What’s important is that you and your partner are on the same page about boundaries.

Disagreements over what’s considered cheating are worth addressing head-on. A transparent conversation about your expectations and boundaries can feel uncomfortable, but it's one of the more protective things you can do for a relationship. A couples therapist can support this conversation if it feels overwhelming to navigate alone.

When you’re talking to your partner about what’s bothering you, try focusing on your own experience rather than their behavior. Something like "I've been feeling distant and want to check in with us" opens the door for an honest conversation instead of a defensive one.

In some cases, trust can be rebuilt after cheating, though it takes consistent effort from both of you. Many couples find professional support helpful along the way.

It usually requires transparency and accountability to understand what led to the breach. Leaving is a valid choice too, as long as the decision is made carefully.
